# Foundational NeRF: Continuous Radiance Fields and Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents one static scene as a continuous MLP-based 5D radiance field: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to view-invariant density and view-dependent RGB color. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency coordinate features, while hierarchical sampling allocates coarse and fine network evaluations along camera rays. For each ray r(t)=o+td, color is the emission–absorption integral of density-weighted radiance multiplied by transmittance; its discrete, differentiable form uses alpha values and ordered alpha compositing. Posed RGB images supervise the MLP through photometric error back-propagated from rendered pixels, without explicit 3D labels in the basic setup. The central design distinction is that the network does not directly generate an image: it predicts local field values, while an analytical volume-rendering procedure integrates those values into pixels. This shared 3D field ties novel views together and makes rendering compatible with gradient-based optimization. The original evidence supports the integrated package—5D MLP field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling—for photorealistic novel-view synthesis under posed-image capture and evaluation settings, rather than isolating any single component as the cause. ## Introduction

This review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than later acceleration, editing, or dynamic-scene variants: first, the continuous 5D scene representation; second, how camera rays query that representation; third, the classical volume-rendering integral and its differentiable discrete approximation; and fourth, the optimization setting in which posed RGB images supervise network weights. The grouping is an explanatory choice for this chapter, not a universal taxonomy of the NeRF literature. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:b4267b040885]

NeRF addresses novel view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous, fully connected neural scene function. The original formulation takes a single 5D coordinate consisting of a 3D spatial location (x, y, z) and a 2D viewing direction (θ, φ), and returns the volume density at that location together with view-dependent emitted radiance or RGB color. In the original paper this is implemented by MLP networks rather than by storing a conventional image, mesh, or dense voxel model. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:b4267b040885]

Density acts as the geometric, view-invariant occupancy-like quantity, while color can depend on viewing direction. This separation lets the same continuous field represent complicated geometry as well as non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights; the original authors note that removing view dependence makes such effects difficult to reproduce. NeRF also applies sinusoidal positional encoding to spatial coordinates and viewing directions before the MLP, and uses hierarchical sampling to concentrate network evaluation where visible scene content is likely. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:12:59963ae78d19:claim:76d1590f86ac]

For rendering, a camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. At a point r(t), the field supplies density σ(r(t)) and color c(r(t),d). The expected ray color is C(r)=∫ T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d)dt, with transmittance T(t)=exp(−∫σ(r(s))ds). Density can be interpreted as the differential probability that the ray terminates at an infinitesimal particle at that location; transmittance records the probability of light having reached that point without absorption or occlusion. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02]

Because this rendering rule is differentiable, NeRF can be optimized from ordinary RGB images with known camera poses. Training casts rays from training viewpoints, queries samples along each ray, numerically accumulates color and density, compares the rendered pixels with observed images, and back-propagates the photometric error into the MLP parameters. The discrete implementation evaluates N samples and approximates each interval as locally constant; a common alpha form uses α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i) and cumulative transmittance from preceding samples. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_1_neural_scene_representations:0:1045b4f41a42:claim:d9cd1c844d34]

A key conceptual point is that the neural network does not directly render an image. It parameterizes the geometry and radiance of one coherent scene, while an analytical, physics-based volume-rendering procedure integrates those quantities along rays. This distinction explains why multi-view renderings are tied to a shared 3D field and why the rendering gradients are suitable for gradient-based optimization. [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:12:9f7dc28545be:claim:10e10eb0b2ae] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:12:9f7dc28545be:claim:db84f725a577]

The scope of this foundational explanation should be distinguished from later objectives. Methods such as hash-grid, voxel, low-rank-tensor, sparse-grid, or other hybrid architectures mainly change how the field is stored or accelerated; dynamic and deformable methods add time, latent codes, or warps; and mip-based formulations alter ray/frustum scale handling. These systems may reuse NeRF-style volume rendering, but their efficiency, animation, anti-aliasing, or editing mechanisms are not required to define the original representation and rendering equation. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:13:74af091c7378:claim:80f789cfaf48] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping of foundational NeRF: (1) the scene field being represented, (2) the coordinates and outputs queried along camera rays, (3) the volume-rendering operator that turns samples into pixels, and (4) the supervision and optimization loop. These are comparison dimensions for explaining the original method, not an exhaustive or paper-authored taxonomy of all neural rendering methods. Later work can be located by which part of this pipeline it changes—storage, sampling, ray geometry, appearance conditioning, dynamics, or rendering acceleration—but such variants should not be conflated with the original representation itself. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_1_neural_scene_representations:0:1045b4f41a42:claim:d9cd1c844d34] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:11f69435bd89]

The first classification criterion is what is being optimized. Foundational NeRF optimizes a continuous, scene-specific neural field implemented by an MLP: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to density and view-dependent color. This differs from methods that learn an encoder–decoder to produce a volume from input images, methods that condition a field on one or few images to learn a cross-scene prior, and methods that store substantial scene state in voxels, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, or hash tables. These alternatives may still use ray integration, but they do not all share the original plain-MLP, per-scene parameterization. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:e532ea43ef3b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23]

A second criterion is the geometric query model. The original NeRF casts one infinitesimal ray per pixel and evaluates point samples r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. Mip-NeRF instead treats the pixel footprint as a conical frustum and encodes scale information in the field query. That distinction is a change to the queried region and scale model, not merely a faster implementation of the same point-ray query. Likewise, methods that trace reflection rays or model more elaborate light transport extend the transport paths beyond the foundational camera-ray accumulation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:1:a3779284c3ef:claim:3a680cb2750e] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:4f475123f295]

A third criterion is how samples become an image. NeRF's defining renderer is differentiable classical volume rendering: each sample contributes color weighted by its alpha and by the transmittance accumulated from earlier samples, so the rendered pixel is a soft, occlusion-aware integral through density. This separates NeRF from direct neural image generation and from hard surface rasterization: the MLP supplies field values, while an analytical ray-marching or volume-integration procedure renders them. Neural Volumes is related in using differentiable ray marching and a learned 3D volume, but its encoder–decoder dynamic-volume construction is a different representation from optimizing a standalone continuous radiance field. [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:12:9f7dc28545be:claim:10e10eb0b2ae] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:1906.07751:section:unknown:0:1bbbbc7cda8d:claim:9bc3c6c960f3] [E:arxiv:1906.07751:abstract:claim:4445dacddafc]

A fourth criterion is the scene and appearance regime addressed by the model. The foundational field is static and uses viewing direction to represent view-dependent radiance within one optimized scene. Deformable- and dynamic-NeRF approaches add canonical spaces, per-observation deformation fields, time-varying latent codes, or modulation so that moving or non-rigid content can be explained. HyperNeRF's review explicitly separates deformation-based approaches, which warp a canonical field, from modulation-based approaches, which condition or alter the radiance field itself. That paper-specific split should be read as a grouping of dynamic variants, not as a taxonomy of static acceleration methods. [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:13:74af091c7378:claim:80f789cfaf48] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:11:c1100a157257:claim:c3e90c0a0be9] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:6ca968e64c50] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:0f0e1e549f77]

Efficiency should be classified separately from representational semantics. Hash tables, multiresolution feature grids, sparse voxel grids, low-rank tensor factorizations, octrees, baked textures or meshes, and improved transmittance estimators primarily target training cost, rendering speed, memory, or sample allocation. They may preserve NeRF-like alpha compositing while replacing the MLP's parameter storage or reducing the number of field evaluations. Conversely, anti-aliasing, dynamic topology, sparse-view priors, editing, text- or exemplar-image control, geometry-oriented training, or physically based scattering address different objectives; faster training is evidence about an implementation trade-off, not by itself evidence that the foundational 5D field or volume-rendering equation has changed. [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:5c2f48945a3e] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:66fffdf9705e] [E:arxiv:2112.05139:abstract:claim:acbccae66b53] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:1bdffa6903bf] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5]

Finally, supervision can be classified by what constrains the field. The original NeRF requires posed RGB images and uses the differentiability of rendered pixels to fit photometric observations, without explicit 3D supervision in the basic setup. Later systems may add learned image-conditioned priors, diffusion priors, depth or mask guidance, jointly optimized camera parameters, inverse optimization for editing, or physically based differentiable renderers for multiple scattering. These methods remain comparable to NeRF only at the level explicitly shared—such as ray-based field queries or differentiable image formation—and should not be treated as directly comparable when their inputs, scene assumptions, transport model, datasets, or learned priors differ. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:e532ea43ef3b] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5]

## Representative Methods

The foundational method is NeRF, a per-scene neural radiance field optimized for novel view synthesis. Its learned object is not an image generator and not an explicit mesh or dense voxel array: it is a continuous scene function implemented in the original work by fully connected MLP networks. Given one 5D coordinate made from a 3D point x=(x,y,z) and a viewing direction d=(θ,φ), the function returns density σ and emitted RGB color c at that point for that direction. The scene is therefore encoded in network weights and queried at arbitrary continuous spatial coordinates rather than being restricted to a fixed discrete grid. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:b4267b040885] The two outputs play different roles. Density is the field's view-independent volumetric quantity and controls where a ray is absorbed or occluded; color is allowed to depend on viewing direction, allowing one coherent geometry model to express non-Lambertian effects such as specular appearance. In the original architecture, the network first processes positional information to produce density and a feature vector, then combines that feature vector with the viewing direction in a later layer to predict view-dependent RGB. This is why changing viewpoint can alter reflected color without requiring a separate geometric model for every image. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] Raw low-dimensional coordinates are difficult for an ordinary MLP to use for detailed scene structure because the network tends to favor low-frequency variation. NeRF addresses this with sinusoidal positional encoding: each coordinate is lifted into a vector containing the original coordinate and sine and cosine terms at increasing frequencies. A later summary writes the spatial encoding as γ(x)=[x, ..., sin(2^kπx), cos(2^kπx), ...], with frequency bands indexed by k. This mapping is applied to spatial coordinates and viewing direction in the original formulation, and it gives the MLP a higher-dimensional input basis from which to reconstruct sharp geometry and appearance. It is a feature transformation, not a separate rendering algorithm. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:12:59963ae78d19:claim:76d1590f86ac] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:0f0e1e549f77]

To form an image, NeRF uses the camera model rather than asking the MLP to output pixels. For a pixel, it defines a camera ray r(t)=o+td with origin o, unit direction d, and near and far bounds t_n and t_f. Points r(t) along this ray are sampled, each point is mapped through positional encoding, and the MLP is evaluated to obtain σ(r(t)) and c(r(t),d). Thus the neural network supplies local physical field values, while a separate classical volume-rendering procedure decides how those local values contribute to the pixel. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:12:9f7dc28545be:claim:10e10eb0b2ae] The continuous rendering rule is an emission-absorption integral. The expected color of ray r is C(r)=∫_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d)dt, where transmittance is T(t)=exp(−∫_{t_n}^{t}σ(r(s))ds). The original paper interprets σ(x) as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at x. Multiplication by T(t) means that a sample's color contributes only to the extent that earlier density along the ray has not already blocked the view; in this soft formulation, partial opacity and semi-transparent structures are represented without assigning a single hard surface intersection. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] On a computer, the integral is approximated by ray marching through ordered samples. With sample spacing Δt_i, queried density σ_i and queried color c_i, a common piecewise-constant approximation uses sample alpha α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i), transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and pixel color Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_i c_i. The ordered accumulation makes earlier samples affect the weight of later samples, and the discrete compositing operation remains differentiable with respect to the colors and densities predicted by the network. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e]

Differentiability is what turns this renderer into a training algorithm. NeRF requires a sparse set of RGB images with known camera poses; it renders rays from those poses, compares the accumulated ray colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the photometric loss through the discrete compositing operation and all MLP evaluations along the rays. No explicit 3D labels are needed in the basic setup: multi-view image consistency, mediated by a shared 3D field and the volume-rendering equation, supervises density and color indirectly. At test time, the same field is queried from new camera poses to synthesize novel views. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_1_neural_scene_representations:0:1045b4f41a42:claim:d9cd1c844d34] The original training procedure uses two levels of samples rather than a single uniform set. A coarse network is evaluated first at broadly distributed samples, and its compositing results are used to form a distribution over ray intervals that places additional fine samples in regions more likely to contain visible scene content. The paper describes this as hierarchical sampling and as a way to allocate MLP capacity toward space containing visible content, instead of spending equal computation on empty space and occupied space. This two-stage allocation is part of the original method's strategy for making the basic implementation effective. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] The essential sampling mechanism is unchanged across the foundational pipeline: choose coordinates along camera rays, query the neural field, alpha-composite the results, and optimize from image error. Additional sampling parameterizations in the original system concern where samples are placed along rays, rather than changing the core 5D field definition, which remains a mapping from position and direction to density and view-dependent color. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b]

A useful way to state the mechanism is that NeRF combines a neural parameterization with a non-neural image-formation step. The MLP does not directly hallucinate a whole view; it predicts local density and radiance at sampled 3D locations. An analytical, physics-based volume renderer integrates those predictions along rays. Later summaries emphasize that this arrangement enforces renderings from one coherent scene model and produces gradients well suited to optimization. It also explains why NeRF can represent thin structures and semi-transport or view-dependent effects better than methods constrained to a single opaque surface per ray. [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:12:9f7dc28545be:claim:10e10eb0b2ae] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:12:9f7dc28545be:claim:db84f725a577] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:6ca968e64c50] The applicability boundary of the foundational formulation is narrower than its rendering principle. The basic NeRF described here is a static, scene-specific model: it must be optimized for a scene from posed images, and its native inputs are spatial location and viewing direction rather than time, text, an exemplar image, or a learned image-conditioned latent. Dynamic methods add deformation fields, per-observation codes, modulation, or higher-dimensional latent coordinates; sparse-view and feed-forward methods add cross-scene priors; editing methods add controllable latent or semantic interfaces. These can build on NeRF, but they introduce assumptions and parameters absent from the original representation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:13:74af091c7378:claim:80f789cfaf48] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:11:c1100a157257:claim:c3e90c0a0be9] [E:arxiv:2112.05139:abstract:claim:acbccae66b53] Likewise, replacing the MLP with sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, voxel grids, or multiresolution hash tables changes the storage and computational architecture, not necessarily the foundational rendering equation. Such representations may retain density, color, ray sampling, and alpha compositing while changing how features are stored and interpolated. Conversely, mip-NeRF changes the query geometry from point samples along an infinitesimal ray to anti-aliased conical frustums, and methods with reflection rays or multiple scattering change light transport. These variants should therefore be understood as modifications to sampling, storage, or transport rather than as the plain original NeRF mechanism. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:1:a3779284c3ef:claim:3a680cb2750e]

The original method's evidence is tied to novel view synthesis from posed images. Its central empirical claim in the cited paper is that optimizing the continuous volumetric function produces state-of-the-art photorealistic novel views of complex scenes compared with prior neural rendering and view-synthesis work. The evidence supports the usefulness of the joint package—5D MLP field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling—under the paper's capture and evaluation settings. It does not by itself establish that the plain MLP is the fastest representation, that it reconstructs reliable surfaces under arbitrary lighting, or that it generalizes across scenes without additional optimization. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:0fa5680ee982] The main computational burden follows directly from the formulation. Because every pixel requires a ray and every ray requires many field evaluations, rendering and optimization can require hundreds of MLP queries per ray. Acceleration papers therefore reduce ray samples, use spatial data structures, bake features into discrete representations, or replace large MLPs with feature grids and small decoders. These approaches target training time, rendering speed, or memory; they are not needed to define the continuous radiance-field concept, but they address a cost intrinsic to repeatedly integrating a neural field along rays. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:66fffdf9705e] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:5c2f48945a3e] Another boundary is geometric and photometric ambiguity. Because image formation is explained by both density and view-dependent radiance, a finite set of views may admit multiple allocations of appearance between geometry and color. NeRF++ discusses this shape-radiance ambiguity, and later geometry-oriented work proposes normalization or additional constraints for non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights. The foundational formulation can produce high-quality rendered images even when its internal density is not being treated as a guaranteed exact surface reconstruction; image reconstruction quality alone should not be read as proof of accurate geometry. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:section:abstract:0:cf232692f549:claim:2c7c41367a9d] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:1bdffa6903bf] The scale model is also limited. Point-sample ray casting can blur or alias when training and testing observations see content at different resolutions or distances; mip-NeRF explicitly identifies this flaw in NeRF's rendering model and replaces the point query with a continuously scaled frustum query. This limitation does not invalidate the original volume-rendering integral, but it shows that the foundational ray-sampling representation assumes a particular scale treatment and is not automatically anti-aliased across multiscale viewing conditions. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:1:a3779284c3ef:claim:3a680cb2750e] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:386e8a07e8e9] Finally, the basic emission-absorption equation is not a full multiple-scattering simulator. It accumulates locally predicted radiance with occlusion along a camera ray, which is effective for ordinary novel-view synthesis but differs from renderers that explicitly model background illumination, scattering inside participating media, traced reflection paths, or other transport effects. Physically based differentiable volume renderers and reflection-ray NeRFs can provide gradients for those richer phenomena, but their additional optics and priors are outside the minimal NeRF formulation. [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:4f475123f295] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:section:abstract:2:b3c9ccfb4665:claim:90f10dbe107d]

In summary, the foundational NeRF mechanism is a continuous 5D MLP field mapping position and viewing direction to density and color, queried along camera rays and integrated by differentiable classical volume rendering. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency expressivity, hierarchical sampling concentrates evaluation in visible regions, and posed RGB images provide supervision through rendered pixel error. Its contribution is a coherent scene representation optimized from images without direct 3D labels; its boundary is that the original model is static, per-scene, computationally sample-heavy, point-ray based, and not by itself a solution to acceleration, dynamics, editing, robust geometry extraction, anti-aliasing, or full light transport. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The empirical comparison relevant to the foundational question is not a head-to-head between two independently proposed NeRF renderers: the original NeRF paper evaluates one integrated method—a continuous 5D MLP radiance field, sinusoidal positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling—on novel-view-synthesis benchmarks using posed RGB images. Its reported result is that this package outperforms prior neural-rendering and view-synthesis methods and produces photorealistic views of scenes with complicated geometry and appearance. The evidence therefore supports the combined formulation under the original capture and evaluation settings; the selected source snippets do not provide matched numerical tables that isolate the rendering equation from the MLP architecture, positional encoding, and sampling strategy. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:b4267b040885]

The training comparison dimension is supervision. Foundational NeRF is optimized per scene from ordinary images with known camera poses, without requiring explicit 3D labels: rays are cast from training cameras, field samples are alpha-composited into predicted pixel colors, and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to the network weights. This differs from feed-forward or conditional systems such as pixelNeRF, which train across scenes on image features and can infer a scene from as few as one view, and from diffusion-guided reconstruction that adds a learned generative prior. Because those methods change the training data, learned priors, and optimization problem, their sparse-view results cannot be ranked against per-scene NeRF as if the input conditions were matched. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:e532ea43ef3b] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5]

A second comparison dimension is the field parameterization used during rendering. The original method stores the scene in basic fully connected networks and repeatedly queries them along rays. Later architectures may instead use sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, voxel features, multiresolution hash tables, baked grids, or hybrid structures while retaining density-color field queries and ray compositing. PVD explicitly frames MLP, sparse-tensor, low-rank-tensor, and hash-table implementations as architectures with different trade-offs and reports any-to-any distillation on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples; for example, it reports distilling an MLP NeRF from a hash-table Instant-NGP teacher 10×–20× faster than training the original NeRF from scratch while reaching superior synthesis quality. That result concerns architecture conversion and training speed/quality in PVD's setup, not a change to the foundational emission-absorption equation. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:7c4e675098ad] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95]

The sampling and ray-geometry comparison is especially important for interpreting later results. Original NeRF casts a single ray per pixel and uses hundreds of point samples; hierarchical sampling first evaluates a coarse network and then allocates more fine samples to intervals with visible content. Mip-NeRF changes the query itself by rendering anti-aliased conical frustums rather than infinitesimal point rays. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF reports a 17% reduction in average error rates while being 7% faster and half the size; on a challenging multiscale variant it reports a 60% error reduction, and it matches a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These figures are evidence for scale-aware anti-aliasing under mip-NeRF's datasets and implementation, not evidence that the original NeRF integral is incorrect for its matched-scale setting. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:1:a3779284c3ef:claim:3a680cb2750e] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:386e8a07e8e9]

Computational-cost comparisons should likewise be tied to the exact acceleration mechanism. The original rendering loop evaluates a large MLP at many samples for each pixel, which acceleration literature identifies as too slow for interactive visualization. SNeRG's baking and deferred-rendering approach is reported to increase NeRF rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but it also introduces a sparse voxel-grid representation with opacity, diffuse color, and learned features plus substantial GPU-memory requirements; NerfAcc reports 1.5×–20× training-time reductions across several NeRF methods by improving sampling through a flexible transmittance-estimator toolbox. These speedups are not directly comparable to each other or to vanilla NeRF quality without matching hardware, resolution, scene sets, memory budgets, sampling counts, and implementation. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:66fffdf9705e] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:9ca817100b6f] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:5c2f48945a3e] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95]

Dynamic-scene comparisons address a different dependent variable. The static foundational NeRF fails when scene content moves; HyperNeRF states this failure explicitly and groups dynamic variants into deformation-based methods that warp a canonical radiance field and modulation-based methods that condition or alter the field using image-related properties. Nerfies similarly adds a canonical template NeRF plus a per-observation deformation field, with elastic and background regularization and coarse-to-fine annealing to handle an under-constrained problem. These systems can be compared with static NeRF on whether they represent motion, but their monocular casual-capture setting and extra regularization make their geometry and appearance results non-comparable to the original static novel-view benchmarks. Geometry-oriented experiments also measure something distinct from photometric novel-view quality. NeRF++ identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity, meaning that view-dependent color and density can jointly explain a finite image set in ways that do not uniquely determine geometry. VDN-NeRF targets this issue under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting, reporting that view-dependence normalization improves geometry without changing the volume-rendering pipeline and can be applied to various baselines, including data captured under a moving light source. Those findings should not be read as a direct PSNR comparison with foundational NeRF: the task includes geometry quality and challenging illumination, and the cited snippets do not supply matched metric values for all methods. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:section:abstract:0:cf232692f549:claim:2c7c41367a9d] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:1bdffa6903bf]

Transport-model comparisons address a different rendering target. The foundational renderer accumulates locally predicted emitted color and density along a camera ray; the selected excerpts do not show it tracing reflection rays or simulating multiple scattering in participating media. Reflection-ray NeRF variants target consistent specular reflections of nearby content while avoiding repeated expensive outgoing-radiance network queries, and physically based differentiable volume renderers coupled with diffusion priors target cloud-like fields where multiple scattering and unknown background radiance matter. In the cloud study, the diffusion prior is trained on 1,000 synthetic volumetric density fields and the renderer supplies gradients for light transport in latent space. Because the optics, priors, datasets, and reconstruction target differ, these results should not be treated as an ordinary bounded static view-synthesis ranking against foundational NeRF. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:4f475123f295] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5]

The available original-paper excerpts provide architectural evidence for view-dependent color: the network uses the input viewing direction to output view-dependent RGB, and the paper states that a model trained without view dependence has difficulty representing specularities. Positional encoding and hierarchical sampling are likewise listed as technical contributions: encoding maps coordinates into higher-dimensional sine and cosine features, and hierarchical sampling directs MLP evaluation toward intervals with visible content. The selected snippets support these mechanism-level descriptions, but they do not provide a fully matched ablation table with separate PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, training-time, and memory values for every component. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:12:59963ae78d19:claim:76d1590f86ac] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b]

Across these comparisons, the consistent experimental boundary is that NeRF's foundational claim is posed for novel-view image fidelity from posed images using a shared static 3D field. Speed numbers from baked, hash-grid, sparse-grid, low-rank, or sampling-accelerated systems concern computational and storage trade-offs; mip-NeRF numbers concern multiscale anti-aliasing; dynamic methods concern temporally varying reconstruction; VDN-NeRF concerns geometry under view-dependent and moving-light conditions; and reflection or scattering renderers concern richer light transport. Because the cited variants differ in datasets, inputs, scene assumptions, priors, sample or hardware settings, metrics, and transport models, their reported results should be read as evidence about their own objectives rather than combined into a single ranking against the original NeRF representation and differentiable volume-rendering formulation. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is computational cost, and it follows directly from the foundational rendering loop. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at ordered 3D samples before density and color can be composited. Acceleration literature describes the original process of evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel as far too slow for interactive visualization; later systems therefore reduce samples, use flexible sampling or transmittance-estimation tools, store features in grids, bake radiance fields, or adopt hash encodings. The cited trade-off is that photorealistic per-scene optimization and high-resolution rendering can require substantial sample-evaluation cost unless the storage, sampling, or network architecture is changed. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:66fffdf9705e] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:5c2f48945a3e]

A second limitation is that the basic model is static and scene-specific. The original NeRF is optimized for one scene from posed images and has no native time coordinate, deformation model, image-conditioning network, or cross-scene prior. HyperNeRF states that although NeRF produces compelling results when all content is static, it fails catastrophically in the presence of moving objects; deformable variants add canonical fields and warps, while modulation-based variants condition or alter the field. Thus the foundational representation should not be treated as a ready solution for moving objects, dynamic topology, casually captured video, or feed-forward reconstruction from one view without additional mechanisms. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:13:74af091c7378:claim:80f789cfaf48] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:11:c1100a157257:claim:c3e90c0a0be9] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:e532ea43ef3b]

The same posed-image supervision that makes NeRF simple also creates an identifiability problem. Density and view-dependent radiance are optimized jointly from RGB observations, so a finite collection of views can sometimes be explained by different allocations between geometry and appearance. NeRF++ explicitly identifies this as shape-radiance ambiguity, and VDN-NeRF argues that under non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights the ambiguity can affect learned geometry even when rendered images look plausible. The practical implication is that high novel-view fidelity is not equivalent to guaranteed accurate surface reconstruction; geometry-sensitive applications may need the normalization proposed by VDN-NeRF or other additional constraints and controlled capture conditions. [E:arxiv:2010.07492:section:abstract:0:cf232692f549:claim:2c7c41367a9d] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:1bdffa6903bf] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b]

Point-ray sampling also leaves a multiscale anti-aliasing limitation. NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and queries point locations; mip-NeRF reports that this model can produce excessive blurring or aliasing when training and testing images observe scene content at different resolutions or distances. Supersampling with many rays is expensive because each ray requires hundreds of MLP queries. Mip-NeRF's conical-frustum solution changes the query region and scale representation, showing that the original point-sample formulation is not automatically scale-aware even though its underlying alpha-compositing rule remains useful. [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:1:a3779284c3ef:claim:3a680cb2750e] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:386e8a07e8e9]

The foundational emission-absorption renderer is also narrower than a general light-transport simulator. It accumulates locally predicted color and density along a camera ray, with transmittance accounting for earlier occlusion, but it does not inherently trace reflection rays or simulate multiple scattering inside participating media. Reflection-oriented NeRF work targets consistent specular reflections of nearby objects by casting additional rays, while physically based differentiable renderers for cloud-like fields explicitly account for multiple scattering and unknown background radiance. Consequently, the basic equation should not be assumed to model complex interreflection or volumetric scattering accurately merely because it handles view-dependent RGB and partial opacity. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:4f475123f295] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5]

Storage and editability create another trade-off in later NeRF architectures. PVD and the accompanying representation discussion distinguish implicit MLP-style fields from explicit or hybrid voxel, sparse-grid, low-rank, and hash-table representations. PVD notes that hash-table-based approaches can train and render faster, but their lack of clear geometric meaning can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing, whereas explicit or hybrid structures can cope better with geometry-aware manipulation. This means that choosing a representation solely for speed can involve a trade-off with interpretability or downstream control. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:a6b83eb02216] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:4:97facdcc473c:claim:04aed354300c] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95]

Camera assumptions are a further practical boundary. The basic optimization loop requires images with known camera poses so that rays can be cast through the correct pixels and compared with observations. Later work summarized in neural-scene-representation surveys addresses inaccurate or unknown extrinsics and intrinsics by jointly optimizing camera parameters, handles unbounded or large-scale scenes with specialized parameterizations, and accounts for blurred input images by modeling the blur process. These extensions indicate that the clean formulation depends on calibration and capture conditions that real datasets may not satisfy. [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_1_neural_scene_representations:0:1045b4f41a42:claim:d9cd1c844d34] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_1_neural_scene_representations:0:1045b4f41a42:claim:ae4d86d5032e] [E:arxiv:2010.07492:section:abstract:0:cf232692f549:claim:2c7c41367a9d]

Sparse and unconstrained observations remain underdetermined without priors. The original method relies on optimizing a separate continuous volume for each scene from a set of calibrated views, whereas pixelNeRF motivates its image-conditioned architecture by noting that independent per-scene optimization requires many calibrated views and substantial compute. When only one or a few views are available, pixelNeRF's sparse-view setting motivates learned image features and a cross-scene scene prior; diffusion-guided systems similarly add a generative prior. These assumptions change the reconstruction problem from minimal per-scene NeRF optimization to prior- or feature-assisted reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:e532ea43ef3b] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:3:604987249f19:claim:556900cfb163]

Finally, the field's success on view synthesis does not imply that its internal representation is universally suitable for every 3D task. Later work notes that NeRF-style implicit fields can deliver excellent rendering while suffering structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation, and dynamic or editing systems add deformation fields, latent codes, mappers, text or exemplar-image controls, or alternative proxies to obtain controllability. The cited consequence is that a representation optimized for rendering may not directly provide the editable geometry or manipulation interfaces required by those downstream systems; foundational NeRF should therefore be understood as a static novel-view-synthesis representation rather than as a complete editing or dynamic-scene solution by itself. [E:arxiv:2507.11971:abstract:claim:734892b7b3a8] [E:arxiv:2112.05139:abstract:claim:acbccae66b53] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:6ca968e64c50] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:1bdffa6903bf]

## Conclusion

In answer to the research question, NeRF's foundational representation is a scene-specific continuous function F(x,d)=(σ,c), where density controls occlusion along rays and color may vary with viewing direction. Camera rays query this function at continuous 3D samples, and the classical renderer forms each pixel by integrating radiance behind accumulated transmittance. The practical differentiable approximation replaces the integral with ordered samples, α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i), and Ĉ(r)=Σ_iT_iα_ic_i, allowing posed-image reconstruction loss to optimize the network weights. The main trade-off is expressivity and simple supervision against cost and scope. The same per-ray neural integration that supports coherent geometry, partial opacity, and view-dependent appearance requires many MLP evaluations per pixel. The basic model is also static, per-scene, point-ray based, calibrated-pose dependent, and not inherently a solution for acceleration, dynamics, anti-aliasing, guaranteed surface extraction, editing, or full multiple-scattering transport; later methods address these objectives by changing storage, sampling, priors, query geometry, deformation, or optics while often retaining NeRF-style compositing.
