Foundational NeRF: Continuous Radiance Fields and Differentiable Volume Rendering

Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents one static scene as a continuous MLP-based 5D radiance field: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to view-invariant density and view-dependent RGB color. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency coordinate features, while hierarchical sampling allocates coarse and fine network evaluations along camera rays. For each ray r(t)=o+td, color is the emission–absorption integral of density-weighted radiance multiplied by transmittance; its discrete, differentiable form uses alpha values and ordered alpha compositing. Posed RGB images supervise the MLP through photometric error back-propagated from rendered pixels, without explicit 3D labels in the basic setup. [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]

The central design distinction is that the network does not directly generate an image: it predicts local field values, while an analytical volume-rendering procedure integrates those values into pixels. This shared 3D field ties novel views together and makes rendering compatible with gradient-based optimization. The original evidence supports the integrated package—5D MLP field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling—for photorealistic novel-view synthesis under posed-image capture and evaluation settings, rather than isolating any single component as the cause. [1], [2], [3], [6]

Introduction

This review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than later acceleration, editing, or dynamic-scene variants: first, the continuous 5D scene representation; second, how camera rays query that representation; third, the classical volume-rendering integral and its differentiable discrete approximation; and fourth, the optimization setting in which posed RGB images supervise network weights. The grouping is an explanatory choice for this chapter, not a universal taxonomy of the NeRF literature. [1]

NeRF addresses novel view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous, fully connected neural scene function. The original formulation takes a single 5D coordinate consisting of a 3D spatial location (x, y, z) and a 2D viewing direction (θ, φ), and returns the volume density at that location together with view-dependent emitted radiance or RGB color. In the original paper this is implemented by MLP networks rather than by storing a conventional image, mesh, or dense voxel model. [1]

Density acts as the geometric, view-invariant occupancy-like quantity, while color can depend on viewing direction. This separation lets the same continuous field represent complicated geometry as well as non-Lambertian appearance such as specular highlights; the original authors note that removing view dependence makes such effects difficult to reproduce. NeRF also applies sinusoidal positional encoding to spatial coordinates and viewing directions before the MLP, and uses hierarchical sampling to concentrate network evaluation where visible scene content is likely. [1], [2]

For rendering, a camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. At a point r(t), the field supplies density σ(r(t)) and color c(r(t),d). The expected ray color is C(r)=∫ T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d)dt, with transmittance T(t)=exp(−∫σ(r(s))ds). Density can be interpreted as the differential probability that the ray terminates at an infinitesimal particle at that location; transmittance records the probability of light having reached that point without absorption or occlusion. [1], [4]

Because this rendering rule is differentiable, NeRF can be optimized from ordinary RGB images with known camera poses. Training casts rays from training viewpoints, queries samples along each ray, numerically accumulates color and density, compares the rendered pixels with observed images, and back-propagates the photometric error into the MLP parameters. The discrete implementation evaluates N samples and approximates each interval as locally constant; a common alpha form uses α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i) and cumulative transmittance from preceding samples. [1], [4], [5]

A key conceptual point is that the neural network does not directly render an image. It parameterizes the geometry and radiance of one coherent scene, while an analytical, physics-based volume-rendering procedure integrates those quantities along rays. This distinction explains why multi-view renderings are tied to a shared 3D field and why the rendering gradients are suitable for gradient-based optimization. [3]

The scope of this foundational explanation should be distinguished from later objectives. Methods such as hash-grid, voxel, low-rank-tensor, sparse-grid, or other hybrid architectures mainly change how the field is stored or accelerated; dynamic and deformable methods add time, latent codes, or warps; and mip-based formulations alter ray/frustum scale handling. These systems may reuse NeRF-style volume rendering, but their efficiency, animation, anti-aliasing, or editing mechanisms are not required to define the original representation and rendering equation. [3], [5], [7], [8]

Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping of foundational NeRF: (1) the scene field being represented, (2) the coordinates and outputs queried along camera rays, (3) the volume-rendering operator that turns samples into pixels, and (4) the supervision and optimization loop. These are comparison dimensions for explaining the original method, not an exhaustive or paper-authored taxonomy of all neural rendering methods. Later work can be located by which part of this pipeline it changes—storage, sampling, ray geometry, appearance conditioning, dynamics, or rendering acceleration—but such variants should not be conflated with the original representation itself. [1], [5], [6]

The first classification criterion is what is being optimized. Foundational NeRF optimizes a continuous, scene-specific neural field implemented by an MLP: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to density and view-dependent color. This differs from methods that learn an encoder–decoder to produce a volume from input images, methods that condition a field on one or few images to learn a cross-scene prior, and methods that store substantial scene state in voxels, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, or hash tables. These alternatives may still use ray integration, but they do not all share the original plain-MLP, per-scene parameterization. [1], [7], [9]

A second criterion is the geometric query model. The original NeRF casts one infinitesimal ray per pixel and evaluates point samples r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. Mip-NeRF instead treats the pixel footprint as a conical frustum and encodes scale information in the field query. That distinction is a change to the queried region and scale model, not merely a faster implementation of the same point-ray query. Likewise, methods that trace reflection rays or model more elaborate light transport extend the transport paths beyond the foundational camera-ray accumulation. [1], [8], [10]

A third criterion is how samples become an image. NeRF's defining renderer is differentiable classical volume rendering: each sample contributes color weighted by its alpha and by the transmittance accumulated from earlier samples, so the rendered pixel is a soft, occlusion-aware integral through density. This separates NeRF from direct neural image generation and from hard surface rasterization: the MLP supplies field values, while an analytical ray-marching or volume-integration procedure renders them. Neural Volumes is related in using differentiable ray marching and a learned 3D volume, but its encoder–decoder dynamic-volume construction is a different representation from optimizing a standalone continuous radiance field. [3], [4], [11]

A fourth criterion is the scene and appearance regime addressed by the model. The foundational field is static and uses viewing direction to represent view-dependent radiance within one optimized scene. Deformable- and dynamic-NeRF approaches add canonical spaces, per-observation deformation fields, time-varying latent codes, or modulation so that moving or non-rigid content can be explained. HyperNeRF's review explicitly separates deformation-based approaches, which warp a canonical field, from modulation-based approaches, which condition or alter the radiance field itself. That paper-specific split should be read as a grouping of dynamic variants, not as a taxonomy of static acceleration methods. [2], [3]

Efficiency should be classified separately from representational semantics. Hash tables, multiresolution feature grids, sparse voxel grids, low-rank tensor factorizations, octrees, baked textures or meshes, and improved transmittance estimators primarily target training cost, rendering speed, memory, or sample allocation. They may preserve NeRF-like alpha compositing while replacing the MLP's parameter storage or reducing the number of field evaluations. Conversely, anti-aliasing, dynamic topology, sparse-view priors, editing, text- or exemplar-image control, geometry-oriented training, or physically based scattering address different objectives; faster training is evidence about an implementation trade-off, not by itself evidence that the foundational 5D field or volume-rendering equation has changed. [5], [7], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]

Finally, supervision can be classified by what constrains the field. The original NeRF requires posed RGB images and uses the differentiability of rendered pixels to fit photometric observations, without explicit 3D supervision in the basic setup. Later systems may add learned image-conditioned priors, diffusion priors, depth or mask guidance, jointly optimized camera parameters, inverse optimization for editing, or physically based differentiable renderers for multiple scattering. These methods remain comparable to NeRF only at the level explicitly shared—such as ray-based field queries or differentiable image formation—and should not be treated as directly comparable when their inputs, scene assumptions, transport model, datasets, or learned priors differ. [1], [4], [9], [16]

Representative Methods

The foundational method is NeRF, a per-scene neural radiance field optimized for novel view synthesis. Its learned object is not an image generator and not an explicit mesh or dense voxel array: it is a continuous scene function implemented in the original work by fully connected MLP networks. Given one 5D coordinate made from a 3D point x=(x,y,z) and a viewing direction d=(θ,φ), the function returns density σ and emitted RGB color c at that point for that direction. The scene is therefore encoded in network weights and queried at arbitrary continuous spatial coordinates rather than being restricted to a fixed discrete grid. [1] The two outputs play different roles. Density is the field's view-independent volumetric quantity and controls where a ray is absorbed or occluded; color is allowed to depend on viewing direction, allowing one coherent geometry model to express non-Lambertian effects such as specular appearance. In the original architecture, the network first processes positional information to produce density and a feature vector, then combines that feature vector with the viewing direction in a later layer to predict view-dependent RGB. This is why changing viewpoint can alter reflected color without requiring a separate geometric model for every image. [1] Raw low-dimensional coordinates are difficult for an ordinary MLP to use for detailed scene structure because the network tends to favor low-frequency variation. NeRF addresses this with sinusoidal positional encoding: each coordinate is lifted into a vector containing the original coordinate and sine and cosine terms at increasing frequencies. A later summary writes the spatial encoding as γ(x)=[x, ..., sin(2^kπx), cos(2^kπx), ...], with frequency bands indexed by k. This mapping is applied to spatial coordinates and viewing direction in the original formulation, and it gives the MLP a higher-dimensional input basis from which to reconstruct sharp geometry and appearance. It is a feature transformation, not a separate rendering algorithm. [1], [2], [3]

To form an image, NeRF uses the camera model rather than asking the MLP to output pixels. For a pixel, it defines a camera ray r(t)=o+td with origin o, unit direction d, and near and far bounds t_n and t_f. Points r(t) along this ray are sampled, each point is mapped through positional encoding, and the MLP is evaluated to obtain σ(r(t)) and c(r(t),d). Thus the neural network supplies local physical field values, while a separate classical volume-rendering procedure decides how those local values contribute to the pixel. [1], [3] The continuous rendering rule is an emission-absorption integral. The expected color of ray r is C(r)=∫{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d)dt, where transmittance is T(t)=exp(−∫{t_n}^{t}σ(r(s))ds). The original paper interprets σ(x) as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at x. Multiplication by T(t) means that a sample's color contributes only to the extent that earlier density along the ray has not already blocked the view; in this soft formulation, partial opacity and semi-transparent structures are represented without assigning a single hard surface intersection. [1], [4] On a computer, the integral is approximated by ray marching through ordered samples. With sample spacing Δt_i, queried density σ_i and queried color c_i, a common piecewise-constant approximation uses sample alpha α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i), transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and pixel color Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_i c_i. The ordered accumulation makes earlier samples affect the weight of later samples, and the discrete compositing operation remains differentiable with respect to the colors and densities predicted by the network. [1], [4]

Differentiability is what turns this renderer into a training algorithm. NeRF requires a sparse set of RGB images with known camera poses; it renders rays from those poses, compares the accumulated ray colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the photometric loss through the discrete compositing operation and all MLP evaluations along the rays. No explicit 3D labels are needed in the basic setup: multi-view image consistency, mediated by a shared 3D field and the volume-rendering equation, supervises density and color indirectly. At test time, the same field is queried from new camera poses to synthesize novel views. [1], [4], [5] The original training procedure uses two levels of samples rather than a single uniform set. A coarse network is evaluated first at broadly distributed samples, and its compositing results are used to form a distribution over ray intervals that places additional fine samples in regions more likely to contain visible scene content. The paper describes this as hierarchical sampling and as a way to allocate MLP capacity toward space containing visible content, instead of spending equal computation on empty space and occupied space. This two-stage allocation is part of the original method's strategy for making the basic implementation effective. [1] The essential sampling mechanism is unchanged across the foundational pipeline: choose coordinates along camera rays, query the neural field, alpha-composite the results, and optimize from image error. Additional sampling parameterizations in the original system concern where samples are placed along rays, rather than changing the core 5D field definition, which remains a mapping from position and direction to density and view-dependent color. [1]

A useful way to state the mechanism is that NeRF combines a neural parameterization with a non-neural image-formation step. The MLP does not directly hallucinate a whole view; it predicts local density and radiance at sampled 3D locations. An analytical, physics-based volume renderer integrates those predictions along rays. Later summaries emphasize that this arrangement enforces renderings from one coherent scene model and produces gradients well suited to optimization. It also explains why NeRF can represent thin structures and semi-transport or view-dependent effects better than methods constrained to a single opaque surface per ray. [2], [3] The applicability boundary of the foundational formulation is narrower than its rendering principle. The basic NeRF described here is a static, scene-specific model: it must be optimized for a scene from posed images, and its native inputs are spatial location and viewing direction rather than time, text, an exemplar image, or a learned image-conditioned latent. Dynamic methods add deformation fields, per-observation codes, modulation, or higher-dimensional latent coordinates; sparse-view and feed-forward methods add cross-scene priors; editing methods add controllable latent or semantic interfaces. These can build on NeRF, but they introduce assumptions and parameters absent from the original representation. [1], [2], [3], [14] Likewise, replacing the MLP with sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, voxel grids, or multiresolution hash tables changes the storage and computational architecture, not necessarily the foundational rendering equation. Such representations may retain density, color, ray sampling, and alpha compositing while changing how features are stored and interpolated. Conversely, mip-NeRF changes the query geometry from point samples along an infinitesimal ray to anti-aliased conical frustums, and methods with reflection rays or multiple scattering change light transport. These variants should therefore be understood as modifications to sampling, storage, or transport rather than as the plain original NeRF mechanism. [5], [7], [8]

The original method's evidence is tied to novel view synthesis from posed images. Its central empirical claim in the cited paper is that optimizing the continuous volumetric function produces state-of-the-art photorealistic novel views of complex scenes compared with prior neural rendering and view-synthesis work. The evidence supports the usefulness of the joint package—5D MLP field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling—under the paper's capture and evaluation settings. It does not by itself establish that the plain MLP is the fastest representation, that it reconstructs reliable surfaces under arbitrary lighting, or that it generalizes across scenes without additional optimization. [1], [6] The main computational burden follows directly from the formulation. Because every pixel requires a ray and every ray requires many field evaluations, rendering and optimization can require hundreds of MLP queries per ray. Acceleration papers therefore reduce ray samples, use spatial data structures, bake features into discrete representations, or replace large MLPs with feature grids and small decoders. These approaches target training time, rendering speed, or memory; they are not needed to define the continuous radiance-field concept, but they address a cost intrinsic to repeatedly integrating a neural field along rays. [5], [12], [13] Another boundary is geometric and photometric ambiguity. Because image formation is explained by both density and view-dependent radiance, a finite set of views may admit multiple allocations of appearance between geometry and color. NeRF++ discusses this shape-radiance ambiguity, and later geometry-oriented work proposes normalization or additional constraints for non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights. The foundational formulation can produce high-quality rendered images even when its internal density is not being treated as a guaranteed exact surface reconstruction; image reconstruction quality alone should not be read as proof of accurate geometry. [15], [17] The scale model is also limited. Point-sample ray casting can blur or alias when training and testing observations see content at different resolutions or distances; mip-NeRF explicitly identifies this flaw in NeRF's rendering model and replaces the point query with a continuously scaled frustum query. This limitation does not invalidate the original volume-rendering integral, but it shows that the foundational ray-sampling representation assumes a particular scale treatment and is not automatically anti-aliased across multiscale viewing conditions. [8], [18] Finally, the basic emission-absorption equation is not a full multiple-scattering simulator. It accumulates locally predicted radiance with occlusion along a camera ray, which is effective for ordinary novel-view synthesis but differs from renderers that explicitly model background illumination, scattering inside participating media, traced reflection paths, or other transport effects. Physically based differentiable volume renderers and reflection-ray NeRFs can provide gradients for those richer phenomena, but their additional optics and priors are outside the minimal NeRF formulation. [10], [16]

In summary, the foundational NeRF mechanism is a continuous 5D MLP field mapping position and viewing direction to density and color, queried along camera rays and integrated by differentiable classical volume rendering. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency expressivity, hierarchical sampling concentrates evaluation in visible regions, and posed RGB images provide supervision through rendered pixel error. Its contribution is a coherent scene representation optimized from images without direct 3D labels; its boundary is that the original model is static, per-scene, computationally sample-heavy, point-ray based, and not by itself a solution to acceleration, dynamics, editing, robust geometry extraction, anti-aliasing, or full light transport. [1], [4]

Comparative Evidence Analysis

The empirical comparison relevant to the foundational question is not a head-to-head between two independently proposed NeRF renderers: the original NeRF paper evaluates one integrated method—a continuous 5D MLP radiance field, sinusoidal positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling—on novel-view-synthesis benchmarks using posed RGB images. Its reported result is that this package outperforms prior neural-rendering and view-synthesis methods and produces photorealistic views of scenes with complicated geometry and appearance. The evidence therefore supports the combined formulation under the original capture and evaluation settings; the selected source snippets do not provide matched numerical tables that isolate the rendering equation from the MLP architecture, positional encoding, and sampling strategy. [1]

The training comparison dimension is supervision. Foundational NeRF is optimized per scene from ordinary images with known camera poses, without requiring explicit 3D labels: rays are cast from training cameras, field samples are alpha-composited into predicted pixel colors, and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to the network weights. This differs from feed-forward or conditional systems such as pixelNeRF, which train across scenes on image features and can infer a scene from as few as one view, and from diffusion-guided reconstruction that adds a learned generative prior. Because those methods change the training data, learned priors, and optimization problem, their sparse-view results cannot be ranked against per-scene NeRF as if the input conditions were matched. [1], [4], [9], [16]

A second comparison dimension is the field parameterization used during rendering. The original method stores the scene in basic fully connected networks and repeatedly queries them along rays. Later architectures may instead use sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, voxel features, multiresolution hash tables, baked grids, or hybrid structures while retaining density-color field queries and ray compositing. PVD explicitly frames MLP, sparse-tensor, low-rank-tensor, and hash-table implementations as architectures with different trade-offs and reports any-to-any distillation on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples; for example, it reports distilling an MLP NeRF from a hash-table Instant-NGP teacher 10×–20× faster than training the original NeRF from scratch while reaching superior synthesis quality. That result concerns architecture conversion and training speed/quality in PVD's setup, not a change to the foundational emission-absorption equation. [1], [5], [7]

The sampling and ray-geometry comparison is especially important for interpreting later results. Original NeRF casts a single ray per pixel and uses hundreds of point samples; hierarchical sampling first evaluates a coarse network and then allocates more fine samples to intervals with visible content. Mip-NeRF changes the query itself by rendering anti-aliased conical frustums rather than infinitesimal point rays. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF reports a 17% reduction in average error rates while being 7% faster and half the size; on a challenging multiscale variant it reports a 60% error reduction, and it matches a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These figures are evidence for scale-aware anti-aliasing under mip-NeRF's datasets and implementation, not evidence that the original NeRF integral is incorrect for its matched-scale setting. [1], [8], [18]

Computational-cost comparisons should likewise be tied to the exact acceleration mechanism. The original rendering loop evaluates a large MLP at many samples for each pixel, which acceleration literature identifies as too slow for interactive visualization. SNeRG's baking and deferred-rendering approach is reported to increase NeRF rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but it also introduces a sparse voxel-grid representation with opacity, diffuse color, and learned features plus substantial GPU-memory requirements; NerfAcc reports 1.5×–20× training-time reductions across several NeRF methods by improving sampling through a flexible transmittance-estimator toolbox. These speedups are not directly comparable to each other or to vanilla NeRF quality without matching hardware, resolution, scene sets, memory budgets, sampling counts, and implementation. [5], [12], [13]

Dynamic-scene comparisons address a different dependent variable. The static foundational NeRF fails when scene content moves; HyperNeRF states this failure explicitly and groups dynamic variants into deformation-based methods that warp a canonical radiance field and modulation-based methods that condition or alter the field using image-related properties. Nerfies similarly adds a canonical template NeRF plus a per-observation deformation field, with elastic and background regularization and coarse-to-fine annealing to handle an under-constrained problem. These systems can be compared with static NeRF on whether they represent motion, but their monocular casual-capture setting and extra regularization make their geometry and appearance results non-comparable to the original static novel-view benchmarks. [2], [3]

Geometry-oriented experiments also measure something distinct from photometric novel-view quality. NeRF++ identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity, meaning that view-dependent color and density can jointly explain a finite image set in ways that do not uniquely determine geometry. VDN-NeRF targets this issue under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting, reporting that view-dependence normalization improves geometry without changing the volume-rendering pipeline and can be applied to various baselines, including data captured under a moving light source. Those findings should not be read as a direct PSNR comparison with foundational NeRF: the task includes geometry quality and challenging illumination, and the cited snippets do not supply matched metric values for all methods. [15], [17]

Transport-model comparisons address a different rendering target. The foundational renderer accumulates locally predicted emitted color and density along a camera ray; the selected excerpts do not show it tracing reflection rays or simulating multiple scattering in participating media. Reflection-ray NeRF variants target consistent specular reflections of nearby content while avoiding repeated expensive outgoing-radiance network queries, and physically based differentiable volume renderers coupled with diffusion priors target cloud-like fields where multiple scattering and unknown background radiance matter. In the cloud study, the diffusion prior is trained on 1,000 synthetic volumetric density fields and the renderer supplies gradients for light transport in latent space. Because the optics, priors, datasets, and reconstruction target differ, these results should not be treated as an ordinary bounded static view-synthesis ranking against foundational NeRF. [1], [4], [10], [16]

The available original-paper excerpts provide architectural evidence for view-dependent color: the network uses the input viewing direction to output view-dependent RGB, and the paper states that a model trained without view dependence has difficulty representing specularities. Positional encoding and hierarchical sampling are likewise listed as technical contributions: encoding maps coordinates into higher-dimensional sine and cosine features, and hierarchical sampling directs MLP evaluation toward intervals with visible content. The selected snippets support these mechanism-level descriptions, but they do not provide a fully matched ablation table with separate PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, training-time, and memory values for every component. [1], [2]

Across these comparisons, the consistent experimental boundary is that NeRF's foundational claim is posed for novel-view image fidelity from posed images using a shared static 3D field. Speed numbers from baked, hash-grid, sparse-grid, low-rank, or sampling-accelerated systems concern computational and storage trade-offs; mip-NeRF numbers concern multiscale anti-aliasing; dynamic methods concern temporally varying reconstruction; VDN-NeRF concerns geometry under view-dependent and moving-light conditions; and reflection or scattering renderers concern richer light transport. Because the cited variants differ in datasets, inputs, scene assumptions, priors, sample or hardware settings, metrics, and transport models, their reported results should be read as evidence about their own objectives rather than combined into a single ranking against the original NeRF representation and differentiable volume-rendering formulation. [1], [5], [8], [15]

Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is computational cost, and it follows directly from the foundational rendering loop. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at ordered 3D samples before density and color can be composited. Acceleration literature describes the original process of evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel as far too slow for interactive visualization; later systems therefore reduce samples, use flexible sampling or transmittance-estimation tools, store features in grids, bake radiance fields, or adopt hash encodings. The cited trade-off is that photorealistic per-scene optimization and high-resolution rendering can require substantial sample-evaluation cost unless the storage, sampling, or network architecture is changed. [1], [4], [5], [12], [13]

A second limitation is that the basic model is static and scene-specific. The original NeRF is optimized for one scene from posed images and has no native time coordinate, deformation model, image-conditioning network, or cross-scene prior. HyperNeRF states that although NeRF produces compelling results when all content is static, it fails catastrophically in the presence of moving objects; deformable variants add canonical fields and warps, while modulation-based variants condition or alter the field. Thus the foundational representation should not be treated as a ready solution for moving objects, dynamic topology, casually captured video, or feed-forward reconstruction from one view without additional mechanisms. [1], [2], [3], [9]

The same posed-image supervision that makes NeRF simple also creates an identifiability problem. Density and view-dependent radiance are optimized jointly from RGB observations, so a finite collection of views can sometimes be explained by different allocations between geometry and appearance. NeRF++ explicitly identifies this as shape-radiance ambiguity, and VDN-NeRF argues that under non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights the ambiguity can affect learned geometry even when rendered images look plausible. The practical implication is that high novel-view fidelity is not equivalent to guaranteed accurate surface reconstruction; geometry-sensitive applications may need the normalization proposed by VDN-NeRF or other additional constraints and controlled capture conditions. [1], [15], [17]

Point-ray sampling also leaves a multiscale anti-aliasing limitation. NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and queries point locations; mip-NeRF reports that this model can produce excessive blurring or aliasing when training and testing images observe scene content at different resolutions or distances. Supersampling with many rays is expensive because each ray requires hundreds of MLP queries. Mip-NeRF's conical-frustum solution changes the query region and scale representation, showing that the original point-sample formulation is not automatically scale-aware even though its underlying alpha-compositing rule remains useful. [8], [18]

The foundational emission-absorption renderer is also narrower than a general light-transport simulator. It accumulates locally predicted color and density along a camera ray, with transmittance accounting for earlier occlusion, but it does not inherently trace reflection rays or simulate multiple scattering inside participating media. Reflection-oriented NeRF work targets consistent specular reflections of nearby objects by casting additional rays, while physically based differentiable renderers for cloud-like fields explicitly account for multiple scattering and unknown background radiance. Consequently, the basic equation should not be assumed to model complex interreflection or volumetric scattering accurately merely because it handles view-dependent RGB and partial opacity. [1], [4], [10], [16]

Storage and editability create another trade-off in later NeRF architectures. PVD and the accompanying representation discussion distinguish implicit MLP-style fields from explicit or hybrid voxel, sparse-grid, low-rank, and hash-table representations. PVD notes that hash-table-based approaches can train and render faster, but their lack of clear geometric meaning can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing, whereas explicit or hybrid structures can cope better with geometry-aware manipulation. This means that choosing a representation solely for speed can involve a trade-off with interpretability or downstream control. [5], [7]

Camera assumptions are a further practical boundary. The basic optimization loop requires images with known camera poses so that rays can be cast through the correct pixels and compared with observations. Later work summarized in neural-scene-representation surveys addresses inaccurate or unknown extrinsics and intrinsics by jointly optimizing camera parameters, handles unbounded or large-scale scenes with specialized parameterizations, and accounts for blurred input images by modeling the blur process. These extensions indicate that the clean formulation depends on calibration and capture conditions that real datasets may not satisfy. [5], [17]

Sparse and unconstrained observations remain underdetermined without priors. The original method relies on optimizing a separate continuous volume for each scene from a set of calibrated views, whereas pixelNeRF motivates its image-conditioned architecture by noting that independent per-scene optimization requires many calibrated views and substantial compute. When only one or a few views are available, pixelNeRF's sparse-view setting motivates learned image features and a cross-scene scene prior; diffusion-guided systems similarly add a generative prior. These assumptions change the reconstruction problem from minimal per-scene NeRF optimization to prior- or feature-assisted reconstruction. [1], [9], [16], [19]

Finally, the field's success on view synthesis does not imply that its internal representation is universally suitable for every 3D task. Later work notes that NeRF-style implicit fields can deliver excellent rendering while suffering structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation, and dynamic or editing systems add deformation fields, latent codes, mappers, text or exemplar-image controls, or alternative proxies to obtain controllability. The cited consequence is that a representation optimized for rendering may not directly provide the editable geometry or manipulation interfaces required by those downstream systems; foundational NeRF should therefore be understood as a static novel-view-synthesis representation rather than as a complete editing or dynamic-scene solution by itself. [2], [14], [15], [20]

Conclusion

In answer to the research question, NeRF's foundational representation is a scene-specific continuous function F(x,d)=(σ,c), where density controls occlusion along rays and color may vary with viewing direction. Camera rays query this function at continuous 3D samples, and the classical renderer forms each pixel by integrating radiance behind accumulated transmittance. The practical differentiable approximation replaces the integral with ordered samples, α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i), and Ĉ(r)=Σ_iT_iα_ic_i, allowing posed-image reconstruction loss to optimize the network weights. [1], [3], [4], [5]

The main trade-off is expressivity and simple supervision against cost and scope. The same per-ray neural integration that supports coherent geometry, partial opacity, and view-dependent appearance requires many MLP evaluations per pixel. The basic model is also static, per-scene, point-ray based, calibrated-pose dependent, and not inherently a solution for acceleration, dynamics, anti-aliasing, guaranteed surface extraction, editing, or full multiple-scattering transport; later methods address these objectives by changing storage, sampling, priors, query geometry, deformation, or optics while often retaining NeRF-style compositing. [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [8], [9], [10], [12], [13], [14], [16], [18]

claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.

RayGauss provides a physically consistent formulation of emitted radiance c and density σ, decomposed with Gaussian functions associated with Spherical Gaussians/Harmonics for all-frequency colorimetric representation.
RayGauss introduces a method enabling differentiable ray casting of irregularly distributed Gaussians using an algorithm that integrates radiance fields slab by slab and leverages a BVH structure.
RayGauss achieves superior rendering quality compared to the state-of-the-art while maintaining reasonable training times.
RayGauss represents radiance fields as a weighted sum of locally supported elliptical basis functions with optimizable positions, orientations, and scales.
RayGauss combines spherical harmonics (SH) and spherical Gaussians (SG) with elliptical basis functions to better represent high-frequency color variations such as specular reflections.
RayGauss's Volume Raycasting algorithm avoids splatting artifacts such as flickering.

RayGauss's ray casting algorithm for sparse basis functions sequentially integrates the radiance field slab-by-slab, accumulating colorimetric properties along the ray in slabs of space corresponding to multiple samples rather than processing individual samples.
RayGauss's ray casting algorithm and its backpropagation rely on a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) implemented on GPU with the OptiX library.
NeRF uses a differentiable Volume Ray Casting algorithm that launches rays in 3D space to compute a discretized version of the volumetric rendering equation using N samples along the ray.

claim_records.text: NeRFMeshing distills a trained NeRF volumetric 3D representation into a Signed Surface Approximation Network, enabling easy extraction of a physically accurate 3D mesh and appearance that can be rendered in real time on an array of devices.
NeRFMeshing introduces a signed surface approximation network (SSAN) that estimates a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) and a feature appearance field.
NeRFMeshing can be leveraged together with any NeRF, without requiring modifications to the NeRF architecture.
NeRFMeshing produces meshes with neural colors having accurate geometry that can be rendered in real time on commodity hardware.
NeRFMeshing does not rely on a fixed grid template during training, enabling reconstruction at any arbitrary resolution afterwards.
NeRFMeshing relies on NeRF networks trained from images, without requiring additional input modalities such as depth.

claim_records.text: NeRF represents a continuous scene as a 5D vector-valued function whose input is a 3D location x=(x,y,z) and 2D viewing direction (θ,φ), and whose output is an emitted color c=(r,g,b) and volume density σ.

NeRF optimizes a deep fully-connected neural network without any convolutional layers (MLP) to represent the 5D scene function by regressing from a single 5D coordinate (x,y,z,θ,φ) to a single volume density and view-dependent RGB color.

NeRF's technical contributions include an approach for representing continuous scenes with complex geometry and materials as 5D neural radiance fields parameterized as basic MLP networks, a differentiable rendering procedure based on classical volume rendering, and a positional encoding to map input 5D coordinates into a higher dimension.
The synthetic Drums scene NeRF visualization uses a set of 100 input views randomly captured on a surrounding hemisphere.

fact_fields.method: NeRF input view capture for synthetic scene

claim_records.text: A model trained without view dependence (only x as input) has difficulty representing specularities, while the full NeRF model uses input viewing direction passed to an additional fully-connected layer with ReLU activation and 128 channels to output view-dependent RGB color.

The expected color C(r) of camera ray r(t)=o+td with near and far bounds tn and tf is computed via volume rendering as C(r) = ∫_{tn}^{tf} T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d)dt, where T(t) = exp(-∫_{tn}^{t} σ(r(s))ds).

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF is represented as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors, rendered using traditional polygon rasterization with a z-buffer to produce per-pixel features interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF textured polygon representation with fragment shader MLP

claim_records.text: Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance, making the rendering process far too slow for interactive visualization.

SNeRG's precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude, but still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid and requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store volumetric textures, prohibiting it from running on common mobile devices.

fact_fields.method: SNeRG sparse voxel grid precomputation and deferred rendering

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF vs SNeRG rendering speed comparison

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF consumes less memory than SNeRG by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling the method to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.

MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all tested devices, as its viewer is an HTML webpage, and allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes as they are simple triangle meshes.
Light fields and Lumigraphs store a dense grid of images enabling real-time rendering of high quality scenes, albeit with limited camera freedom and significant storage overhead.

Point-based representations that refine scene geometry while training post-processing networks often result in a lack of 3D consistency, require powerful desktop GPUs, and have not been demonstrated to run on a mobile device.

fact_fields.method: Point-based neural rendering with post-processing CNN

claim_records.text: DefTet differentiably renders a tetrahedral grid with occupancy and color at each vertex, then composites interpolated values at all intersected faces along a ray, incurring a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.

NVDiffRec combines differentiable marching tetrahedra with differentiable rasterization to perform full inverse rendering and extract triangle meshes, materials, and lighting from images, enabling elaborate editing and scene relighting, but incurs a significant loss in view-synthesis quality.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that enables any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.
PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations, from shallower to deeper, to enable fast architecture conversions.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model achieves a 10×~20× faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving superior synthesis quality.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.
PVD employs special treatment of density to deal with its specific numerical instability problem during distillation.

A NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality compared to a NeRF model trained from scratch using 25 hours on the Family and Barn scene from TanksAndTemples dataset.
Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (INGP) utilizes multilevel hash tables for effective compression of feature tensors.

Methods with explicit or hybrid NeRF representations usually enjoy faster training due to shallower representations and cope better with geometric-aware editing like merging and other scene manipulations, in contrast to purely implicit representations.

PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures, and employs special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping to improve training stability and synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric radiance field representation that creates color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.

CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning, and represents scenes via foreground and background decomposition for 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
Pix2NeRF introduces a pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, built upon π-GAN, and employs an unsupervised approach that can be trained with independent images.
Pix2NeRF is currently restricted to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, taking a continuous 5D coordinate as input and outputting volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.

NeRF introduces positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation, and can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities using input viewing direction.

claim_records.text: The proposed single-view volumetric field reconstruction technique models the unknown distribution of volumetric fields using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.

fact_fields.method: unconditional diffusion model for volumetric field distribution modeling

claim_records.text: The neural diffusion model is trained on the latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly, monoplanar representation.

fact_fields.method: diffusion model training on monoplanar representation latent codes

claim_records.text: A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space, making reconstructions better aligned with observed data compared to classic NeRF approaches.

The reconstruction of internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and presence of vanishing gradients, and this limitation can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR) toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field, with controlled variations in the diffusion step by considering the gradient of the image loss with respect to the learned latent space representation.

fact_fields.method: multi-resolution hybrid encoding neural radiance field (Hyb-NeRF)

claim_records.text: Cone tracing-based features embedded in the learnable positional encoding eliminate encoding ambiguity and reduce aliasing artifacts.

claim_records.text: Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show Hyb-NeRF achieves faster rendering speed with better rendering quality and lower memory footprint compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
On the ficus scene in Blender, Hyb-NeRF with 16.4M parameters achieves 35.85 PSNR and 0.986 SSIM, outperforming JNGP with 24.4M parameters which achieves 33.23 PSNR and 0.981 SSIM.

Hash-based multi-resolution grid representation has trainable features at coarse resolution levels with lower resolutions and less compression than fine-level feature grids, resulting in limited representation power and low memory efficiency.

fact_fields.method: analysis of hash-based multi-resolution grid representation properties

claim_records.text: All Hyb-NeRF models can reconstruct high-quality radiance fields in 9 minutes.

The smallest Hyb-NeRF model with 8.4M trainable parameters takes 4 minutes to achieve better rendering quality than state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially less memory than previous and concurrent voxel-based methods.

claim_records.text: Mip-NeRF matches the accuracy of a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the presented multiscale dataset while being 22× faster.

Mip-NeRF reasons about the 3D conical frustum defined by a camera pixel and featurizes it using integrated positional encoding (IPE), which approximates the frustum with a multivariate Gaussian and computes the closed-form integral E[γ(x)] over positional encodings of coordinates within the Gaussian.

fact_fields.method: integrated positional encoding (IPE) over conical frustum

claim_records.text: NeRF training minimizes the sum of squared differences between all input pixel values and all predicted pixel values using gradient descent, and trains two separate MLPs (coarse and fine) to improve sample efficiency.

Mip-NeRF extends NeRF to represent the scene at a continuously-valued scale by efficiently rendering anti-aliased conical frustums instead of rays, reducing objectionable aliasing artifacts and improving fine detail representation.
Mip-NeRF is 7% faster than NeRF and has half the size of NeRF.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 17% on the dataset presented with NeRF.
Compared to NeRF, mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 60% on a challenging multiscale variant of the NeRF dataset.
Mip-NeRF merges the separate coarse and fine MLPs used by NeRF for hierarchical sampling into a single MLP, resulting in approximately 7% faster speed than NeRF and half as many parameters.

IPE preserves frequencies that are constant over an interval and softly removes frequencies that vary over an interval, effectively producing anti-aliased positional encoding features that smoothly encode the size and shape of a volume of space.
For each pixel being rendered, mip-NeRF casts a cone instead of a ray, samples n+1 values for t_k, and computes IPE features for the interval spanning each adjacent pair of sampled t_k values.
NeRF's rendering model can cause excessive blurring and aliasing because it casts a single ray through each pixel and queries an MLP at samples along that ray.

claim_records.text: Fourier PlenOctrees suffer from artifacts introduced by involved compression when combined with recent state-of-the-art techniques for training static per-frame NeRF models.

The proposed FPO++ density encoding adapts Fourier-based compression to the characteristics of the transfer function used by the underlying volume rendering procedure, leading to a substantial reduction of artifacts in the dynamic model.
FPO++ augments training data to relax the periodicity assumption of the Fourier compression used in Fourier PlenOctrees.
PlenOctrees use a hierarchical octree structure of density and view-dependent radiance in terms of spherical harmonics (SH) to entirely avoid network evaluations during rendering.
Instant-NGP incorporated a multi-resolution hash encoding to significantly accelerate the training of neural models including NeRF.
Prior discrete scene representation acceleration methods including Instant-NGP, Plenoxels, and TensoRF are limited to static scenes only and do not account for dynamic scenarios like motion.
NeRF synthesizes novel views using volume rendering of density and view-dependent radiance optimized in an implicit neural scene representation using MLPs from a set of posed images.
Some NeRF variants reduce aliasing artifacts by modeling volumetric rendering with conical frustums instead of rays.
Fourier PlenOctrees (FPO) extend ordinary PlenOctrees by combining them with the Fourier transform, enabling efficient handling of time-variant density and SH-based radiance for dynamic scenes.
During FPO construction, compression is performed on encoded densities σ' = e_comp(e_log(σ)), where the encoding consists of a component-dependent part and a logarithmic part.

The proposed component-dependent and logarithmic density encoding allows better reconstruction of original densities without fine-tuning than can be achieved with only DFT and IDFT as used in standard FPO.

fact_fields.method: component-dependent + logarithmic density encoding vs DFT/IDFT only

claim_records.text: The logarithmic density encoding is defined as e_log(σ) = log(σ + 1), chosen so that e_log remains a non-negative function for non-negative input densities with e_log(0) = 0.
The logarithmic density encoding focuses Fourier approximation on densities near or equal to zero, since larger density values are mapped closer together while smaller values stay almost the same.

After applying the inverse of the logarithmic encoding after IDFT during rendering, the L2-error in fine-tuning is allowed to be larger for encoded high density values than without logarithmic encoding, focusing optimization on more important reconstruction parts.

claim_records.text: NerfDiff distills knowledge from a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) into NeRF by synthesizing and refining a set of virtual views at test time.
NerfDiff significantly outperforms existing NeRF-based and geometry-free approaches on the ShapeNet, ABO, and Clevr3D datasets.
NerfDiff jointly trains a camera-space triplane-based NeRF together with a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) on a collection of scenes at the training stage.
A naive finetuning strategy that optimizes NeRF parameters directly using CDM outputs leads to subpar renderings because CDM outputs tend to be multi-view inconsistent.

fact_fields.method: naive NeRF finetuning using CDM outputs

claim_records.text: NerfDiff's NeRF-guided distillation updates the NeRF representation and guides the multi-view diffusion process in an alternating fashion.
NerfDiff introduces an efficient image-conditioned NeRF representation based on camera-aligned triplanes that enables efficient rendering and finetuning from the CDM.
NerfDiff's 3D-aware CDM integrates volume rendering into 2D diffusion models to facilitate generalization to novel views.
Diffusion-based generative models have become state-of-the-art on image synthesis tasks.
Existing generalizable NeRF models conditioned by projection of 3D points and gathering of corresponding image features yield blurry results when target views are far from the input view.

fact_fields.method: generalizable NeRF models conditioned on projected 3D point image features

claim_records.text: NeRF requires tens or hundreds of images for overfitting a scene and has no generalization ability to infer new scenes.
Existing approaches leveraging 2D generative models to predict novel views conditioned on an input view are only able to synthesize partially 3D-consistent images.

fact_fields.method: 2D generative model-based novel view synthesis conditioned on input view

A naive finetuning strategy that optimizes NeRF parameters directly using CDM outputs leads to subpar renderings because CDM outputs tend to be multi-view inconsistent.
NerfDiff's NeRF-guided distillation updates the NeRF representation and guides the multi-view diffusion process in an alternating fashion.
NerfDiff introduces an efficient image-conditioned NeRF representation based on camera-aligned triplanes that enables efficient rendering and finetuning from the CDM.
NerfDiff's 3D-aware CDM integrates volume rendering into 2D diffusion models to facilitate generalization to novel views.
Diffusion-based generative models have become state-of-the-art on image synthesis tasks.
Existing generalizable NeRF models conditioned by projection of 3D points and gathering of corresponding image features yield blurry results when target views are far from the input view.
NeRF requires tens or hundreds of images for overfitting a scene and has no generalization ability to infer new scenes.
Existing approaches leveraging 2D generative models to predict novel views conditioned on an input view are only able to synthesize partially 3D-consistent images.

claim_records.text: EvaSurf can be trained in just 1-2 hours using a single GPU.
EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS.
The final rendering package required for EvaSurf takes up only 40-50 MB.
EvaSurf employs an efficient surface-based model with a multi-view supervision module to ensure accurate mesh reconstruction.
EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.
EvaSurf uses a lightweight neural shader with explicit geometry and implicit texture to support real-time rendering on common mobile devices.
EvaSurf can reconstruct high-quality appearance and accurate mesh on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
EvaSurf's training procedure is 10× faster than MobileNeRF.
EvaSurf's final rendering package storage is much smaller than existing methods including MobileNeRF.
NeRF-based methods require plenty of sampling points to forward a deep MLP network, requiring massive computation that is impractical for mobile devices.

Recent Gaussian-based methods achieve high-quality rendering with high efficiency by optimizing explicit representations, but fail to render at interactive framerates on mobile devices due to large disk storage requirements and lack of mobile-end optimization.
EvaSurf incorporates view-aware encoding into an implicit texture to assign different weights to dimensions of the view-aware texture, modeling appearance with view-dependent effects.
EvaSurf runs on common devices including PCs, tablets, and mobile phones with over 40 FPS.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieves impressive view synthesis results for 360° capture of bounded scenes and forward-facing capture of bounded and unbounded scenes.

NeRF fits multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) representing view-invariant opacity and view-dependent color volumes to a set of training images, and samples novel views based on volume rendering techniques.
The NeRF++ method improves view synthesis fidelity for 360° captures of objects within large-scale, unbounded 3D scenes by addressing a parametrization issue.
An artificially constructed shape-radiance ambiguity solution is a valid NeRF reconstruction that perfectly fits input images but has very limited novel view synthesis ability.
Accurately generating a novel view from the degenerate shape-radiance ambiguity solution would require reconstructing an arbitrarily complex view-dependent function at each surface point.

The degenerate shape-radiance ambiguity model is very unlikely to accurately interpolate the complex view-dependent function unless training views are extremely dense, as in conventional light field rendering works.

NeRF avoids degenerate shape-radiance ambiguity solutions due to two related factors: incorrect geometry forces the radiance field to have higher intrinsic complexity, and NeRF's specific MLP structure implicitly encodes a smooth BRDF prior on surface reflectance.
As opacity σ deviates from the correct shape, radiance c must generally become a high-frequency function with respect to viewing direction d to reconstruct input images.
For the correct shape, the surface light field will generally be much smoother, and constant for Lambertian materials.
The higher complexity required for incorrect shapes is more difficult to represent with a limited capacity MLP.
NeRF's specific MLP structure encodes an implicit prior favoring smooth surface reflectance functions where radiance c is smooth with respect to viewing direction d at any given surface point x.

NeRF's MLP treats scene position x and viewing direction d asymmetrically: d is injected close to the end of the MLP, resulting in fewer MLP parameters and fewer non-linear activations involved in creating view-dependent effects.
In NeRF, the opacity field σ is computed as a function of 3D position x ∈ R³, and the radiance field c is parameterized by both 3D position x and viewing direction d ∈ S².

Replacing NeRF's radiance field model c with a vanilla MLP that treats x and d symmetrically (accepting both as inputs to the first layer and encoding both with γ₁₀(·)) results in reduced test image quality compared with NeRF's special MLP on DTU scenes.

claim_records.text: NeRF yields blurred rendering results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts if test images are taken in distant views.

Mip-NeRF proposes a multiscale representation as a conical frustum to encode scale information, but is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).

Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture for real-time anti-aliasing rendering, including a density Mip-VoG for scene geometry and a feature Mip-VoG with a small MLP for view-dependent color.

Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials and uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

claim_records.text: pixelNeRF is a learning framework that predicts a continuous neural scene representation conditioned on one or few input images.
pixelNeRF introduces an architecture that conditions a NeRF on image inputs in a fully convolutional manner.
pixelNeRF can perform novel view synthesis in a feed-forward manner from a sparse set of views, as few as one.
pixelNeRF can be trained directly from images with no explicit 3D supervision, leveraging the volume rendering approach of NeRF.

pixelNeRF outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines for novel view synthesis and single image 3D reconstruction on ShapeNet benchmarks for held-out objects and entire unseen categories, multi-object ShapeNet scenes, and real scenes from the DTU dataset.
pixelNeRF outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines for novel view synthesis and single image 3D reconstruction on multi-object ShapeNet scenes and real scenes from the DTU dataset.
NeRF encodes a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field f that returns a differential density σ and RGB color c for a 3D point x and viewing direction unit vector d.
The NeRF volumetric radiance field is rendered into a 2D image via the integral ˆC(r) = ∫ tf tn T(t)σ(t)c(t)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫ t tn σ(s) ds) handles occlusion.
In pixelNeRF, the world point x with view direction d is transformed into each input view i's coordinate system using the world to camera transform as x(i) = P(i)x, d(i) = R(i)d.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model.
CLIP-NeRF allows manipulating NeRF using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.
CLIP-NeRF introduces a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved via applying a learned deformation field to the positional encoding, and color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.

CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update the latent codes to reflect the targeted editing, trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to the latent codes for manipulation to enable editing on real images.

claim_records.text: Tetra-NeRF uses an adaptive tetrahedral representation obtained via Delaunay triangulation, built on an available sparse point cloud of the scene, instead of uniform voxel subdivision or point-based representations.
The tetrahedral representation used by Tetra-NeRF enables efficient training and leads to state-of-the-art results.
Compared to voxel-based NeRF representations, Tetra-NeRF's tetrahedral representation provides more detail around scene parts likely to be close to the surface.
Compared to point-based NeRF representations, Tetra-NeRF's tetrahedral approach achieves better performance.

claim_records.text: UE4-NeRF partitions each large scene into different sub-NeRFs to support real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.

For each partitioned independent scene, UE4-NeRF initializes polygonal meshes by constructing multiple regular octahedra within the scene, with polygonal face vertices continuously optimized during training.
Drawing inspiration from Level of Detail (LOD) techniques, UE4-NeRF trains meshes of varying levels of detail for different observation levels.
Combined with the rasterization pipeline in Unreal Engine 4 (UE4), UE4-NeRF achieves real-time rendering of large-scale scenes at 4K resolution with a frame rate of up to 43 FPS.
Rendering within UE4 facilitates subsequent-stage scene editing for UE4-NeRF.
Experiments demonstrate that UE4-NeRF achieves rendering quality comparable to state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: NeRF trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates representing spatial location and viewing direction into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance.
NeRF is only applicable to static scenes where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF considers time as an additional input to the system, and splits the learning process into two main stages: one that encodes the scene into a canonical space and another that maps this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
Once the networks are trained, D-NeRF can render novel images, controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus, the object movement.
D-NeRF demonstrates effectiveness on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.
D-NeRF applies the encoder γ(·) independently to each coordinate and camera view component, using L = 10 for x, and L = 4 for d and t.
In D-NeRF, the 3D point p(h, t) denotes the point on the camera ray x(h) transformed to canonical space using the Deformation Network Ψt.
In D-NeRF, density σ and color c are predicted by the Canonical Network Ψx.
NeRF multilayer perceptron networks can encode the mapping from 5D inputs representing spatial locations (x, y, z) and camera views (θ, φ) to emitted radiance values and volume density.
NeRF learned mapping allows free-viewpoint rendering with extraordinary realism.
D-NeRF learns a displacement field ∆x that maps all points x of the scene to a common canonical configuration.
In D-NeRF, the volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance for the canonical configuration is learned and transferred to the original input points to render novel views.
D-NeRF can learn a volumetric density representation for continuous non-rigid scenes trained with a single view per time instant.
The D-NeRF Canonical Network is an MLP Ψx(x, d) that maps a 3D point x and a view direction d to its emitted color c and volume density σ, trained to encode the scene in the canonical configuration.
The D-NeRF Deformation Network is an MLP Ψt(x, t) that predicts a deformation field defining the transformation between the scene at time t and the scene in its canonical configuration.

claim_records.text: NeRF performance drops significantly when the number of input views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in the estimated scene geometry, and by divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF addresses sparse-input NeRF artifacts by regularizing the geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and annealing the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other methods that optimize over a single scene, and in many cases also conditional models that are extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: NeRF and its variants require lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for a single scene.
NSVF still requires many training hours due to the deep MLP in its hybrid representation, despite using an octree to avoid redundant MLP queries in free space.
The density activation used for voxel density is shifted softplus: σ = softplus(σ̈) = log(1 + exp(σ̈ + b)), where b is a hyperparameter.

Using softplus instead of ReLU as the density activation is crucial for directly optimizing voxel density, as ReLU irreparably sets voxels to negative values while softplus allows exploring density very close to 0.

claims: The proposed voxel grid optimization approach achieves NeRF-comparable quality and converges from scratch in less than 15 minutes using a single GPU.
The proposed method takes about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene on five inward-facing benchmarks, matching or surpassing NeRF's quality.

In the fine stage, view-dependent color emission is modeled using an explicit-implicit hybrid representation consisting of a feature voxel grid and a shallow MLP.
NeRF and its variants require lengthy training time ranging from hours to days for a single scene.
NSVF still requires many training hours due to the deep MLP in its hybrid representation, despite using an octree to avoid redundant MLP queries in free space.
The density activation used for voxel density is shifted softplus: σ = softplus(σ̈) = log(1 + exp(σ̈ + b)), where b is a hyperparameter.

Using softplus instead of ReLU as the density activation is crucial for directly optimizing voxel density, as ReLU irreparably sets voxels to negative values while softplus allows exploring density very close to 0.

claim_records.text: NeRF has low rendering efficiency due to the need for multiple network forwardings to render a single pixel.
Neural Light Fields (NeLF) reduce the computation cost of NeRF by querying only one single network forwarding per pixel.
Existing NeLF methods require significantly larger network capacities to achieve close visual quality to NeRF, which limits their rendering efficiency in practice.
The proposed Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in NeLF.
NeRDF models the radiance distribution along each ray with frequency basis and predicts frequency weights using the network, with pixel values computed via volume rendering on radiance distributions.
NeRDF achieves a ~254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.

claim_records.text: Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific and lack universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
All existing 3D representations inherently struggle with the trade-off between data complexity and fidelity.

The introduced 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized (tree-structured) proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation, and offers scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects, whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent NeRF works have improved ability to render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination, but are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.
Recent NeRF techniques for specular appearance rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The NeRF-Casting approach casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.

fact_fields.method: Ray tracing through NeRF representation with reflection ray casting and small color-decoding network

claim_records.text: The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.

NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes, while requiring comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.
