claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model.
CLIP-NeRF allows manipulating NeRF using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.
CLIP-NeRF introduces a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance.
In CLIP-NeRF, shape conditioning is achieved via applying a learned deformation field to the positional encoding, and color conditioning is deferred to the volumetric rendering stage.

CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update the latent codes to reflect the targeted editing, trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to the latent codes for manipulation to enable editing on real images.

claim_records.text: Tetra-NeRF uses an adaptive tetrahedral representation obtained via Delaunay triangulation, built on an available sparse point cloud of the scene, instead of uniform voxel subdivision or point-based representations.
The tetrahedral representation used by Tetra-NeRF enables efficient training and leads to state-of-the-art results.
Compared to voxel-based NeRF representations, Tetra-NeRF's tetrahedral representation provides more detail around scene parts likely to be close to the surface.
Compared to point-based NeRF representations, Tetra-NeRF's tetrahedral approach achieves better performance.

claim_records.text: UE4-NeRF partitions each large scene into different sub-NeRFs to support real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.

For each partitioned independent scene, UE4-NeRF initializes polygonal meshes by constructing multiple regular octahedra within the scene, with polygonal face vertices continuously optimized during training.
Drawing inspiration from Level of Detail (LOD) techniques, UE4-NeRF trains meshes of varying levels of detail for different observation levels.
Combined with the rasterization pipeline in Unreal Engine 4 (UE4), UE4-NeRF achieves real-time rendering of large-scale scenes at 4K resolution with a frame rate of up to 43 FPS.
Rendering within UE4 facilitates subsequent-stage scene editing for UE4-NeRF.
Experiments demonstrate that UE4-NeRF achieves rendering quality comparable to state-of-the-art approaches.

claim_records.text: NeRF trains a deep network to map 5D input coordinates representing spatial location and viewing direction into a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance.
NeRF is only applicable to static scenes where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF considers time as an additional input to the system, and splits the learning process into two main stages: one that encodes the scene into a canonical space and another that maps this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
Once the networks are trained, D-NeRF can render novel images, controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus, the object movement.
D-NeRF demonstrates effectiveness on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.
D-NeRF applies the encoder γ(·) independently to each coordinate and camera view component, using L = 10 for x, and L = 4 for d and t.
In D-NeRF, the 3D point p(h, t) denotes the point on the camera ray x(h) transformed to canonical space using the Deformation Network Ψt.
In D-NeRF, density σ and color c are predicted by the Canonical Network Ψx.
NeRF multilayer perceptron networks can encode the mapping from 5D inputs representing spatial locations (x, y, z) and camera views (θ, φ) to emitted radiance values and volume density.
NeRF learned mapping allows free-viewpoint rendering with extraordinary realism.
D-NeRF learns a displacement field ∆x that maps all points x of the scene to a common canonical configuration.
In D-NeRF, the volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance for the canonical configuration is learned and transferred to the original input points to render novel views.
D-NeRF can learn a volumetric density representation for continuous non-rigid scenes trained with a single view per time instant.
The D-NeRF Canonical Network is an MLP Ψx(x, d) that maps a 3D point x and a view direction d to its emitted color c and volume density σ, trained to encode the scene in the canonical configuration.
The D-NeRF Deformation Network is an MLP Ψt(x, t) that predicts a deformation field defining the transformation between the scene at time t and the scene in its canonical configuration.

NeRF is only applicable to static scenes where the same spatial location can be queried from different images.

D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to a dynamic domain, allowing reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single camera moving around the scene.

D-NeRF considers time as an additional input to the system, and splits the learning process into two main stages: one that encodes the scene into a canonical space and another that maps this canonical representation into the deformed scene at a particular time.
Both mappings in D-NeRF are simultaneously learned using fully-connected networks.
Once the networks are trained, D-NeRF can render novel images, controlling both the camera view and the time variable, and thus, the object movement.
D-NeRF demonstrates effectiveness on scenes with objects under rigid, articulated and non-rigid motions.
D-NeRF applies the encoder γ(·) independently to each coordinate and camera view component, using L = 10 for x, and L = 4 for d and t.
In D-NeRF, the 3D point p(h, t) denotes the point on the camera ray x(h) transformed to canonical space using the Deformation Network Ψt.
In D-NeRF, density σ and color c are predicted by the Canonical Network Ψx.
NeRF multilayer perceptron networks can encode the mapping from 5D inputs representing spatial locations (x, y, z) and camera views (θ, φ) to emitted radiance values and volume density.
NeRF learned mapping allows free-viewpoint rendering with extraordinary realism.
D-NeRF learns a displacement field ∆x that maps all points x of the scene to a common canonical configuration.
In D-NeRF, the volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance for the canonical configuration is learned and transferred to the original input points to render novel views.
D-NeRF can learn a volumetric density representation for continuous non-rigid scenes trained with a single view per time instant.
The D-NeRF Canonical Network is an MLP Ψx(x, d) that maps a 3D point x and a view direction d to its emitted color c and volume density σ, trained to encode the scene in the canonical configuration.
The D-NeRF Deformation Network is an MLP Ψt(x, t) that predicts a deformation field defining the transformation between the scene at time t and the scene in its canonical configuration.

claim_records.text: NeRF performance drops significantly when the number of input views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in the estimated scene geometry, and by divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF addresses sparse-input NeRF artifacts by regularizing the geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and annealing the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other methods that optimize over a single scene, and in many cases also conditional models that are extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: NeRF has low rendering efficiency due to the need for multiple network forwardings to render a single pixel.
Neural Light Fields (NeLF) reduce the computation cost of NeRF by querying only one single network forwarding per pixel.
Existing NeLF methods require significantly larger network capacities to achieve close visual quality to NeRF, which limits their rendering efficiency in practice.
The proposed Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in NeLF.
NeRDF models the radiance distribution along each ray with frequency basis and predicts frequency weights using the network, with pixel values computed via volume rendering on radiance distributions.
NeRDF achieves a ~254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.

claim_records.text: VQ-NeRF reduces the sampling space of NeRF to a lower resolution and reinstates it to the original size using a pre-trained VAE decoder to mitigate the sampling time bottleneck during rendering.
VQ-NeRF uses a multi-scale NeRF sampling scheme that concurrently optimizes the NeRF model at both compressed and original scales to enhance the network's ability to preserve fine details.
VQ-NeRF incorporates a semantic loss function to improve the geometric fidelity and semantic coherence of 3D reconstructions.
Evaluation on the DTU, BlendMVS, and H3DS datasets confirms the superior performance of VQ-NeRF.

claim_records.text: Optimizing and rendering Neural Radiance Fields is computationally expensive due to the vast number of samples required by volume rendering.
Improved sampling is generally applicable across NeRF variants under an unified concept of transmittance estimator.
NerfAcc is a Python toolbox that provides flexible APIs for incorporating advanced sampling methods into NeRF related methods.
NerfAcc can reduce the training time of several recent NeRF methods by 1.5x to 20x with minimal modifications to the existing codebase.
Highly customized NeRFs, such as Instant-NGP, can be implemented in native PyTorch using NerfAcc.
Recent NeRF works that include alternative sampling approaches often do not focus on sampling as a core aspect of their work.

claim_records.text: Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific and lack universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
All existing 3D representations inherently struggle with the trade-off between data complexity and fidelity.

The introduced 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized (tree-structured) proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation, and offers scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation, and offers scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) typically struggle to reconstruct and render highly specular objects, whose appearance varies quickly with changes in viewpoint.
Recent NeRF works have improved ability to render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination, but are unable to synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.
Recent NeRF techniques for specular appearance rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The NeRF-Casting approach casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors which are decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance at those points.

fact_fields.method: Ray tracing through NeRF representation with reflection ray casting and small color-decoding network

claim_records.text: The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.

NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes, while requiring comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: The Nerfies method decomposes a non-rigidly deforming scene into a template volume represented as a neural radiance field (NeRF) and a per-observation deformation field that associates a point in observation coordinates to a point on the template.
Jointly optimizing a NeRF together with a deformation field leads to an under-constrained optimization problem.

fact_fields.method: Joint optimization of NeRF and deformation field

claim_records.text: Nerfies introduces an elastic regularization on the deformation, a background regularization, and a continuous coarse-to-fine annealing technique to address the under-constrained optimization problem and avoid bad local minima.

fact_fields.method: Elastic deformation regularization, background regularization, continuous coarse-to-fine annealing

claim_records.text: NeRF uses a neural network to encode color and density as a function of location and viewing angle, and generates novel views using volume rendering.

Nerfies generalizes NeRF by using a canonical NeRF model as a template for all observations, supplemented by a per-observation deformation field represented as an MLP conditioned on a per-image learned latent code that warps 3D points from observation coordinates to the canonical model frame.
A neural radiance field (NeRF) is a continuous volumetric function F: (x, d, ψi) → (c, σ) which maps a 3D position x and viewing direction d to a color c and density σ.

NeRF maps inputs x and d using a sinusoidal positional encoding γ: R3 → R3+6m defined as γ(x) = [x, ···, sin(2^k πx), cos(2^k πx), ···], where m is a hyper-parameter controlling the total number of frequency bands and k ∈ {0, ..., m−1}.

fact_fields.method: Sinusoidal positional encoding for NeRF inputs

claim_records.text: Coupled with volume rendering techniques, NeRFs can represent scenes with photo-realistic quality.

fact_fields.method: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with volume rendering

claim_records.text: Nerfies is the first method capable of photorealistically reconstructing deformable scenes using photos/videos captured casually from mobile phones.
Nerfies augments NeRF by optimizing an additional continuous volumetric deformation field that warps each observed point into a canonical 5D NeRF.
NeRF-like deformation fields are prone to local minima, and Nerfies proposes a coarse-to-fine optimization method for coordinate-based models that allows for more robust optimization.

fact_fields.method: Coarse-to-fine optimization for coordinate-based deformable NeRF models

claim_records.text: Nerfies proposes an elastic regularization of the deformation field adapted from principles of geometry processing and physical simulation, which further improves optimization robustness.

fact_fields.method: Elastic deformation regularization adapted from geometry processing and physical simulation

claim_records.text: Nerfies can turn casually captured selfie photos/videos into deformable NeRF models that allow for photorealistic renderings of the subject from arbitrary viewpoints, which are dubbed "nerfies".
Nerfies evaluation uses time-synchronized data collected with a rig of two mobile phones, yielding train/validation images of the same pose at different viewpoints.

fact_fields.method: Data collection using two-mobile-phone synchronized rig

claim_records.text: Nerfies faithfully reconstructs non-rigidly deforming scenes and reproduces unseen views with high fidelity.

The Nerfies deformation network takes a position-encoded position γ_α(x) using coarse-to-fine annealing parameterized by α, along with a deformation code ω, and outputs a deformed position x′; its architecture is identical across all experiments.
The Nerfies canonical NeRF network is identical to the original NeRF MLP, except it provides an appearance latent code ψ along with the view direction to modulate appearance as in the NeRF-A model.
NSFF models dynamic scenes by directly conditioning NeRF with a position-encoded time variable γ(t), modulating color, density, and a scene-flow prediction.
Nerfies differs from NSFF in that Nerfies uses a deformation field while NSFF directly modulates NeRF density by conditioning it with γ(t).

fact_fields.method: Comparative analysis between Nerfies and NSFF

claim_records.text: Nerfies differs from NSFF in that Nerfies uses a per-example latent code to condition each observation while NSFF uses a position-encoded time variable γ(t).

fact_fields.method: Comparative analysis between Nerfies and NSFF

claim_records.text: Nerfies differs from NSFF in that NSFF uses depth from MI-DAS and optical flow from RAFT as supervision while Nerfies only uses a photometric loss.

fact_fields.method: Comparative analysis between Nerfies and NSFF

claim_records.text: Nerfies uses the official code released by NSFF authors, with hyper-parameters tuned for Nerfies' datasets, for quantitative comparison with NSFF.

fact_fields.method: Quantitative comparison using official NSFF code with author-provided tuned hyper-parameters

claim_records.text: The proposed LLNeRF approach enhances scene representation and synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from sRGB low-light images in an unsupervised manner.
The core of LLNeRF is a decomposition of radiance field learning that allows joint enhancement of illumination, noise reduction, and distorted color correction with the NeRF optimization process.
LLNeRF produces novel view images with proper lighting and vivid colors and details given a collection of camera-finished low dynamic range (8-bits/channel) images from a low-light scene.
Experiments demonstrate that the LLNeRF method outperforms existing low-light enhancement methods and NeRF methods.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.
Human images captured from random camera angles present challenges for high-quality 3D human reconstruction.
SHERF is the first generalizable Human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image.
SHERF extracts and encodes 3D human representations in canonical space, enabling rendering and animation from free views and poses.

fact_fields.method: SHERF canonical space 3D human representation encoding

claim_records.text: SHERF uses a bank of 3D-aware hierarchical features including global, point-level, and pixel-aligned features to facilitate informative encoding.
Global features in SHERF enhance the information extracted from the single input image and complement the information missing from the partial 2D observation.
Point-level features in SHERF provide strong clues of 3D human structure.
Pixel-aligned features in SHERF preserve more fine-grained details.
SHERF uses a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance, with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

claim_records.text: HyperNeRF lifts NeRFs into a higher dimensional space, representing the 5D radiance field for each input image as a slice through this hyper-space.
Compared to Nerfies, HyperNeRF reduces average error rates by 4.1% for interpolation as measured by LPIPS.
Compared to Nerfies, HyperNeRF reduces average error rates by 8.6% for novel-view synthesis as measured by LPIPS.
NeRF uses a conventional multilayer perceptron (MLP) to parameterize volumetric density and color as a function of spatial scene coordinates.

In NeRF, an analytical physics-based volumetric rendering engine is used to render a scene whose geometry and radiance are parameterized by a neural network, rather than using a neural network to directly render an image.

NeRF variants for dynamic scenes are separated into two categories: deformation-based approaches that apply spatially-varying deformation to a canonical radiance field, and modulation-based approaches that directly condition the radiance field on input image properties.

NeRF represents a scene as a continuous volumetric field of density and radiance, defined as function F: (x, d, ψi) → (c, σ) parameterized by an MLP, mapping 3D position x and viewing direction d to color c and density σ.
NeRF maps input coordinates x and d using sinusoidal positional encoding before providing them to the MLP.

HyperNeRF extends the domain of the template NeRF to a higher dimensional space (x, w) ∈ R^(3+W), where W is the number of higher dimensions, with the template NeRF represented as MLP F: (x, w, d, ψi) → (c, σ).
HyperNeRF associates a latent deformation code ωi and a latent appearance code ψi with each image i.

In HyperNeRF, samples x along rays are concatenated with the image's latent deformation code ωi and provided as input to MLPs parameterizing a deformation field, which yields a warped coordinate x' and a slicing surface in hyperspace that produces ambient coordinate w.

In HyperNeRF, the concatenation of (x', w), viewing direction d, and appearance code ψi are used as inputs to the MLP parameterizing the template NeRF, with densities and colors integrated along the ray via volumetric rendering.

NeRF variants for dynamic scenes are separated into two categories: deformation-based approaches that apply spatially-varying deformation to a canonical radiance field, and modulation-based approaches that directly condition the radiance field on input image properties.

NeRF represents a scene as a continuous volumetric field of density and radiance, defined as function F: (x, d, ψi) → (c, σ) parameterized by an MLP, mapping 3D position x and viewing direction d to color c and density σ.
NeRF maps input coordinates x and d using sinusoidal positional encoding before providing them to the MLP.

HyperNeRF extends the domain of the template NeRF to a higher dimensional space (x, w) ∈ R^(3+W), where W is the number of higher dimensions, with the template NeRF represented as MLP F: (x, w, d, ψi) → (c, σ).
HyperNeRF associates a latent deformation code ωi and a latent appearance code ψi with each image i.

In HyperNeRF, samples x along rays are concatenated with the image's latent deformation code ωi and provided as input to MLPs parameterizing a deformation field, which yields a warped coordinate x' and a slicing surface in hyperspace that produces ambient coordinate w.

In HyperNeRF, the concatenation of (x', w), viewing direction d, and appearance code ψi are used as inputs to the MLP parameterizing the template NeRF, with densities and colors integrated along the ray via volumetric rendering.

claim_records.text: Deformable Neural Mesh Primitive (DNMP) is a flexible and compact neural variant of classic mesh representation that combines rasterization-based rendering efficiency with neural representation capability for photo-realistic image synthesis.
A DNMP consists of a set of connected deformable mesh vertices with paired vertex features to parameterize the geometry and radiance information of a local area.
DNMP enforces the shape of each primitive to be decoded from a relatively low-dimensional latent space to constrain optimization degrees of freedom and lower storage budgets.
DNMP rendering colors are decoded from vertex features interpolated with rasterization by a view-dependent MLP.
DNMP achieves leading performance for novel view synthesis in urban scenarios.
DNMP enables fast rendering at 2.07ms per 1k pixels.
DNMP has low peak memory usage of 110MB per 1k pixels.
The lightweight DNMP version runs 33 times faster than vanilla NeRFs.
The lightweight DNMP variant has rendering speed of 0.61ms per 1k pixels, comparable to highly-optimized Instant-NGP at 0.71ms per 1k pixels.

claim_records.text: mip-NeRF 360 reduces mean-squared error by 57% compared to mip-NeRF on unbounded real-world scenes.
mip-NeRF achieves an SSIM of 0.526 on the unbounded scene shown in Figure 1.
The proposed mip-NeRF 360 model achieves an SSIM of 0.804 on the unbounded scene shown in Figure 1.
The total capacity of the mip-NeRF 360 model is approximately 15 times larger than that of mip-NeRF.
The training time of mip-NeRF 360 only increases modestly, by approximately 2 times, relative to mip-NeRF.
When scaling NeRF from objects to buildings, Martin-Brualla et al. doubled the number of MLP hidden units and increased the number of MLP evaluations by 8 times.
The ray is rendered using evenly-spaced coarse distances sampled from a uniform distribution spanning the camera's near and far planes.
The proposal MLP in mip-NeRF 360 predicts volumetric density but does not predict color, and its weights are supervised by the histogram weights generated by the NeRF MLP.

claim_records.text: IBRNet synthesizes novel views by blending pixels from nearby images with weights and volume densities inferred by an MLP and ray transformer network.
IBRNet can be trained end-to-end with an L2 loss on reconstructed image colors.
IBRNet does not use positional encoding to regress colors, instead blending colors from source views.
IBRNet achieves substantially better SSIM and LPIPS than NeRF on the Real Forward-Facing dataset.
NeRF requires a lengthy optimization process per new scene, taking hours or days to converge, before synthesizing novel views.
IBRNet aggregates 2D latent features from nearby source views for each sampled 3D location along a ray to produce a density feature indicating surface presence.

claim_records.text: 3DGS is introduced into indoor 3D Object Detection for the first time in this work.
3DGS primarily relies on 2D pixel-level supervision, resulting in unclear 3D spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs and poor differentiation between objects and background, which hinders indoor 3DOD.
2D images typically include numerous background pixels, leading to densely reconstructed 3DGS with many noisy Gaussian blobs representing the background, negatively affecting detection.
Incorporating 2D Boundary Guidance significantly enhances the spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs, resulting in clearer differentiation between objects and their background.

The Box-Focused Sampling strategy uses 2D boxes to generate object probability distribution in 3D space, allowing effective probabilistic sampling in 3D to retain more object blobs and reduce noisy background blobs.
3DGS-DET outperforms NeRF-Det++ by +6.0 on mAP@0.25 for the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET outperforms NeRF-Det++ by +7.8 on mAP@0.5 for the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET outperforms NeRF-Det++ by +14.9 on mAP@0.25 for the ARKITScenes dataset.

claim_records.text: NeRF operates exclusively on radiance (the product of reflectance and illumination) and does not explicitly perform scene decomposition into shape, reflectance and illumination.
NeRD, a NeRF extension, can perform reflectance decomposition but struggles to accurately recover detailed illumination, thereby significantly limiting realism.
The proposed reflectance decomposition network can estimate shape, BRDF, and per-image illumination given a set of object images captured under varying illumination.
Neural-PIL is an illumination integration network that replaces a costly illumination integral operation in the rendering with a simple network query.
Deep low-dimensional priors on BRDF and illumination representations are learned using novel smooth manifold auto-encoders.
The proposed decompositions result in considerably better BRDF and light estimates, enabling more accurate novel view-synthesis and relighting compared to prior art.

fact_fields.method: proposed reflectance decomposition network with Neural-PIL

claim_records.text: Plenoxels represent a scene as a sparse 3D grid with spherical harmonics and can be optimized from calibrated images via gradient methods and regularization without any neural components.
On standard benchmark tasks, Plenoxels are optimized two orders of magnitude faster than Neural Radiance Fields with no loss in visual quality.
Plenoxels can render novel viewpoints at interactive rates of 15 fps with its non-fast-rendering-optimized implementation, and can be converted into a PlenOctree for faster rendering.
Direct optimization of Plenoxels' fully explicit 3D model achieves more than a 100× speedup over NeRF++ for training, reducing training time to roughly 4 days for NeRF++ baseline.

NeRF requires several days for full training and about half a minute to render a full image, because every rendered pixel requires evaluating the coordinate-based MLP at hundreds of sample locations along the corresponding ray.
NeRF's training lasts more than a day and rendering requires 30 seconds per frame on a single GPU.

Plenoxels is an explicit volumetric representation based on a view-dependent sparse voxel grid without any neural networks, optimized end-to-end from calibrated 2D photographs using differentiable rendering loss on training views and a total variation regularizer.
PlenOctrees extract a NeRF variant into a sparse voxel grid in which each voxel represents view-dependent color using spherical harmonics.
Both JAXNeRF and Plenoxel models exhibit artifacts in the synthetic drums scene, but the specific artifacts differ, with some artifacts unavoidable for any underdetermined inverse problem.

claim_records.text: NeuDA is a flexible neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids for high-fidelity surface reconstruction.
NeuDA maintains hierarchical anchor grids where each vertex stores a 3D position (or anchor) instead of a direct embedding (or feature).
NeuDA optimizes anchor grids such that different local geometry structures can be adaptively encoded.
NeuDA introduces a simple hierarchical positional encoding method for the hierarchical anchor structure to flexibly exploit properties of high-frequency and low-frequency geometry and appearance.
Experiments on the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets demonstrate that NeuDA can produce promising mesh surfaces.

Vlastelica et al. introduce combinatorial building blocks into neural networks, and the end-to-end trainable network can generate informative backward gradients through any black-box implementations of combinatorial solvers.
Rolínek et al. design an end-to-end network that incorporates a combinatorial solver to solve the graph matching problem, based on combinatorial building blocks.
Li uses a tensor-SIFT based EMD to tackle the contour tracking problem.
Gould et al. present methods for differentiation through optimization problems with only equality constraints.
Agrawal et al. propose a method that can compute the gradient of the solution with respect to the coefficients in the convex cone program, which can scale to large problems.
Barratt describes the general case of using the implicit function theorem and interior point methods to compute the Jacobian of the solution with respect to the problem parameters.

Amos and Kolter design a batched Quadratic Programming solver as a layer that can be integrated into a neural network for end-to-end training, using the implicit function theorem and interior point methods theory.

claim_records.text: HollowNeRF delivers comparable rendering quality to Instant-NGP while utilizing just 31% of the parameters.
HollowNeRF can achieve a PSNR accuracy gain of up to 1dB using only 56% of the parameters.

HollowNeRF trains a coarse 3D saliency mask that guides efficient feature pruning, and employs an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) pruner to sparsify the 3D saliency mask during training.
By exploiting sparsity in the 3D scene to redistribute hash collisions, HollowNeRF improves rendering quality while using a fraction of the parameters of comparable state-of-the-art solutions.

Existing hashgrid-based NeRF solutions for culling unnecessary feature grid regions rely on prior knowledge of object shape or periodically estimate object shape during training via repeated model evaluations, which are costly and wasteful.

fact_fields.method: existing hashgrid-based NeRF feature grid culling solutions

claim_records.text: The explicit 3D Gaussian volume compression model achieves significant training speed and reconstruction quality improvements on both structured and unstructured volumes compared to existing INRs.
The explicit 3D Gaussian volume compression model enables compression ratios much higher than previous work for unstructured volumes.
Existing INRs for unstructured volumes do not encode geometry, requiring partial mesh storage for later sampling and limiting achievable compression.
The explicit 3D Gaussian volume model naturally encodes domain geometry, eliminating the need for mesh storage in unstructured volumes and introducing significantly higher compression opportunities.
The explicit 3D Gaussian volume model uses a sampling strategy that reconstructs scalar values at spatial locations through weighted aggregation of intersecting Gaussians.

The explicit 3D Gaussian volume model includes optimized CUDA-accelerated pipelines for structured and unstructured model sampling, loss functions that encourage accurate domain coverage, and a novel sampling-error based densification strategy.

claim_records.text: Most prior neural rendering works following the original NeRF require an expensive per-scene optimization process.
MVSNeRF leverages deep MVS techniques to achieve across-scene neural radiance field estimation for view synthesis using only few images as input.
MVSNeRF's entire framework models a neural radiance field, regressing volume density and view-dependent radiance in the scene from few (three) input images.
Once the scene encoding volume S is reconstructed, this volume combined with the MLP decoder A can be used independently without the prepending 2D and 3D CNNs.

MVSNeRF reconstructs a neural encoding volume and regresses volume density and view-dependent radiance at arbitrary points in a scene, enabling applying differentiable volume rendering to regress images colors.
The physically based volume rendering equation can be numerically evaluated via differentiable ray marching for view synthesis.
A pixel's radiance value (color) is computed by marching a ray through the pixel and accumulating radiance at sampled shading points on the ray.
MVSNeRF as a radiance field function provides the volume rendering properties σk and rk for the ray marching.
The ray marching rendering in MVSNeRF is fully differentiable, allowing the framework to regress final pixel colors at novel viewpoints using the three input views from end to end.
MVSNeRF supervises its entire framework with groundtruth pixel colors using an L2 rendering loss.
MVSNeRF estimates a neural scene encoding volume that consists of per-voxel neural features encoding information about the local scene geometry and appearance.
MVSNeRF uses a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to decode the volume density and radiance at arbitrary continuous locations using tri-linearly interpolated neural features inside the encoding volume.
Once estimated, the encoding volume can be used directly (dropping the 3D CNN) for final rendering by differentiable ray marching.
Compared with existing MVS methods, MVSNeRF enables differentiable neural rendering that allows for training without 3D supervision and inference time optimization for further quality improvement.

Compared with existing neural rendering works, MVSNeRF's MVS-like architecture is natural to conduct cross-view correspondence reasoning, facilitating generalization to unseen testing scenes and leading to better neural scene reconstruction and rendering.
The high-frequency details in MVSNeRF can be recovered in an augmented volume via a fast per-scene fine-tuning optimization.
Given an arbitrary 3D location x and a viewing direction d, MVSNeRF uses an MLP A to regress the corresponding volume density σ and view-dependent radiance r from the neural encoding volume S.

MVSNeRF considers pixel colors c = [I(ui, vi)] from the original images Ii as additional input, where (ui, vi) is the pixel location when projecting the 3D point x onto view i, and c concatenates the colors I(ui, vi) from all views as a 3M-channel vector.

MVSNeRF is expressed as a function of a radiance field: σ, Rad = MVSNeRF(Pos, Dir; Img_i, Cam_i), where x represents a 3D location, d is a viewing direction, σ is the volume density at x, and r is the output radiance (RGB color) at x depending on the viewing direction d.
The output volume properties from MVSNeRF's network can be directly used to synthesize a novel image It at a novel target viewpoint Φt via differentiable ray marching.
MVSNeRF considers a sparse set of nearby input views for efficient radiance field reconstruction, using M = 3 views for its experiments.
MVSNeRF first builds a cost volume at the reference view (view i = 1) by warping 2D neural features onto multiple sweeping planes.
MVSNeRF leverages a 3D CNN to reconstruct the neural encoding volume, and uses an MLP to regress volume rendering properties, expressing a radiance field.

assertions.source_quote: Foundational NeRF represents one static scene as a continuous MLP-based 5D radiance field: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to view-invariant density and view-dependent RGB color. Positional encoding supplies high-frequency coordinate features, while hierarchical sampling allocates more evaluations to intervals likely to contain visible content. Camera rays query this field, and an analytical emission–absorption renderer integrates density and color. The continuous color is the transmittance-weighted integral of σ(r(t))c(r(t),d); its discrete, differentiable form uses α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i), accumulated transmittance, and alpha-weighted color compositing. Posed RGB images supervise the MLP through photometric pixel error without explicit 3D labels in the basic setup. assertions.source_quote: For rendering, a camera ray is written as r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. At a point r(t), the field supplies density σ(r(t)) and color c(r(t),d). assertions.source_quote: For this review, the organizing choice is a pipeline-based grouping of foundational NeRF: (1) the scene field being represented, (2) the coordinates and outputs queried along camera rays, (3) the volume-rendering operator that turns samples into pixels, and (4) the supervision and optimization loop. These are comparison dimensions for explaining the original method, not an exhaustive or paper-authored taxonomy of all neural rendering methods. Later work can be located by which part of this pipeline it changes—storage, sampling, ray geometry, appearance conditioning, dynamics, or rendering acceleration—but such variants should not be conflated with the original representation itself. assertions.source_quote: The first classification criterion is what is being optimized. Foundational NeRF optimizes a continuous, scene-specific neural field implemented by an MLP: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to density and view-dependent color. This differs from methods that learn an encoder–decoder to produce a volume from input images, methods that condition a field on one or few images to learn a cross-scene prior, and methods that store substantial scene state in voxels, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, triplanes, or hash tables. These alternatives may still use ray integration, but they do not all share the original plain-MLP, per-scene parameterization. assertions.source_quote: A second criterion is the geometric query model. The original NeRF casts one infinitesimal ray per pixel and evaluates point samples r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. Mip-NeRF instead treats the pixel footprint as a conical frustum and uses integrated positional encoding so that scale and aliasing are represented during the field query. That distinction is a change to the queried region and scale model, not merely a faster implementation of the same point-ray query. Likewise, methods that trace reflection rays or model more elaborate light transport extend the transport paths beyond the foundational camera-ray accumulation. assertions.source_quote: A third criterion is how samples become an image. NeRF's defining renderer is differentiable classical volume rendering: each sample contributes color weighted by its alpha and by the transmittance accumulated from earlier samples, so the rendered pixel is a soft, occlusion-aware integral through density. This separates NeRF from direct neural image generation and from hard surface rasterization: the MLP supplies field values, while an analytical ray-marching or volume-integration procedure renders them. Neural Volumes is related in using differentiable ray marching and a learned 3D volume, but its encoder–decoder dynamic-volume construction is a different representation from optimizing a standalone continuous radiance field. assertions.source_quote: A fourth criterion is the scene and appearance regime addressed by the model. The foundational field is static and uses viewing direction to represent view-dependent radiance within one optimized scene. Deformable- and dynamic-NeRF approaches add canonical spaces, per-observation deformation fields, time-varying latent codes, or modulation so that moving or non-rigid content can be explained. HyperNeRF's review explicitly separates deformation-based approaches, which warp a canonical field, from modulation-based approaches, which condition or alter the radiance field itself. That paper-specific split should be read as a grouping of dynamic variants, not as a taxonomy of static acceleration methods. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency should be classified separately from representational semantics. Hash tables, multiresolution feature grids, sparse voxel grids, low-rank tensor factorizations, octrees, baked textures or meshes, and improved transmittance estimators primarily target training cost, rendering speed, memory, or sample allocation. They may preserve NeRF-like alpha compositing while replacing the MLP's parameter storage or reducing the number of field evaluations. Conversely, anti-aliasing, dynamic topology, sparse-view priors, editing, language control, geometry normalization, or physically based scattering address different objectives; faster training is evidence about an implementation trade-off, not by itself evidence that the foundational 5D field or volume-rendering equation has changed. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency should be classified separately from representational semantics. Hash tables, multiresolution feature grids, sparse voxel grids, low-rank tensor factorizations, octrees, baked textures or meshes, and improved transmittance estimators primarily target training cost, rendering speed, memory, or sample allocation. assertions.source_quote: Finally, supervision can be classified by what constrains the field. The original NeRF requires posed RGB images and uses the differentiability of rendered pixels to fit photometric observations, without explicit 3D supervision in the basic setup. Later systems may add learned image-conditioned priors, diffusion priors, depth or mask guidance, jointly optimized camera parameters, inverse optimization for editing, or physically based differentiable renderers for multiple scattering. These methods remain comparable to NeRF only at the level explicitly shared—such as ray-based field queries or differentiable image formation—and should not be treated as directly comparable when their inputs, scene assumptions, transport model, datasets, or learned priors differ. assertions.source_quote: Raw low-dimensional coordinates are difficult for an ordinary MLP to use for detailed scene structure because the network tends to favor low-frequency variation. NeRF addresses this with sinusoidal positional encoding: each coordinate is lifted into a vector containing the original coordinate and sine and cosine terms at increasing frequencies. A later summary writes the spatial encoding as γ(x)=[x, ..., sin(2^kπx), cos(2^kπx), ...], with frequency bands indexed by k. This mapping is applied to spatial coordinates and viewing direction in the original formulation, and it gives the MLP a higher-dimensional input basis from which to reconstruct sharp geometry and appearance. It is a feature transformation, not a separate rendering algorithm. assertions.source_quote: The continuous rendering rule is an emission-absorption integral. The expected color of ray r is C(r)=∫_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)σ(r(t))c(r(t),d)dt, where transmittance is T(t)=exp(−∫_{t_n}^{t}σ(r(s))ds). The original paper interprets σ(x) as the differential probability of a ray terminating at an infinitesimal particle at x. assertions.source_quote: Differentiability is what turns this renderer into a training algorithm. NeRF requires a sparse set of RGB images with known camera poses; it renders rays from those poses, compares the accumulated ray colors with observed pixel colors, and back-propagates the photometric loss through the discrete compositing operation and all MLP evaluations along the rays. No explicit 3D labels are needed in the basic setup: multi-view image consistency, mediated by a shared 3D field and the volume-rendering equation, supervises density and color indirectly. At test time, the same field is queried from new camera poses to synthesize novel views. assertions.source_quote: A useful way to state the mechanism is that NeRF combines a neural parameterization with a non-neural image-formation step. The MLP does not directly hallucinate a whole view; it predicts local density and radiance at sampled 3D locations. An analytical, physics-based volume renderer integrates those predictions along rays. Later summaries emphasize that this arrangement enforces renderings from one coherent scene model and produces gradients well suited to optimization. It also explains why NeRF can represent thin structures and semi-transport or view-dependent effects better than methods constrained to a single opaque surface per ray. assertions.source_quote: The applicability boundary of the foundational formulation is narrower than its rendering principle. The basic NeRF described here is a static, scene-specific model: it must be optimized for a scene from posed images, and its native inputs are spatial location and viewing direction rather than time, text, an exemplar image, or a learned image-conditioned latent. Dynamic methods add deformation fields, per-observation codes, modulation, or higher-dimensional latent coordinates; sparse-view and feed-forward methods add cross-scene priors; editing methods add controllable latent or semantic interfaces. These can build on NeRF, but they introduce assumptions and parameters absent from the original representation. assertions.source_quote: The main computational burden follows directly from the formulation. Because every pixel requires a ray and every ray requires many field evaluations, rendering and optimization can require hundreds of MLP queries per ray. Acceleration papers therefore reduce ray samples, use spatial data structures, bake features into discrete representations, or replace large MLPs with feature grids and small decoders. These approaches target training time, rendering speed, or memory; they are not needed to define the continuous radiance-field concept, but they address a cost intrinsic to repeatedly integrating a neural field along rays. assertions.source_quote: Another boundary is geometric and photometric ambiguity. Because image formation is explained by both density and view-dependent radiance, a finite set of views may admit multiple allocations of appearance between geometry and color. NeRF++ discusses this shape-radiance ambiguity, and later geometry-oriented work proposes normalization or additional constraints for non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights. The foundational formulation can produce high-quality rendered images even when its internal density is not being treated as a guaranteed exact surface reconstruction; image reconstruction quality alone should not be read as proof of accurate geometry. assertions.source_quote: The training comparison dimension is supervision. Foundational NeRF is optimized per scene from ordinary images with known camera poses, without requiring explicit 3D labels: rays are cast from training cameras, field samples are alpha-composited into predicted pixel colors, and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to the network weights. This differs from feed-forward or conditional systems such as pixelNeRF, which train across scenes on image features and can infer a scene from as few as one view, and from diffusion-guided reconstruction that adds a learned generative prior. Because those methods change the training data, learned priors, and optimization problem, their sparse-view results cannot be ranked against per-scene NeRF as if the input conditions were matched. assertions.source_quote: The training comparison dimension is supervision. Foundational NeRF is optimized per scene from ordinary images with known camera poses, without requiring explicit 3D labels: rays are cast from training cameras, field samples are alpha-composited into predicted pixel colors, and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to the network weights. This differs from feed-forward or conditional systems such as pixelNeRF, which train across scenes on image features and can infer a scene from as few as one view, and from diffusion-guided reconstruction that adds a learned generative prior. Because those methods change the training data, learned priors, and optimization problem, their sparse-view results cannot be ranked against per-scene NeRF as if the input conditions were matched. assertions.source_quote: A second comparison dimension is the field parameterization used during rendering. The original method stores the scene in basic fully connected networks and repeatedly queries them along rays. Later architectures may instead use sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, voxel or tri-plane features, multiresolution hash tables, baked grids, or hybrid structures while retaining density-color field queries and ray compositing. PVD explicitly frames MLP, sparse-tensor, low-rank-tensor, and hash-table implementations as architectures with different trade-offs and reports any-to-any distillation on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples; for example, it reports distilling an MLP NeRF from a hash-table Instant-NGP teacher 10×–20× faster than training the original NeRF from scratch while reaching superior synthesis quality. That result concerns architecture conversion and training speed/quality in PVD's setup, not a change to the foundational emission-absorption equation. assertions.source_quote: A second comparison dimension is the field parameterization used during rendering. The original method stores the scene in basic fully connected networks and repeatedly queries them along rays. Later architectures may instead use sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, voxel or tri-plane features, multiresolution hash tables, baked grids, or hybrid structures while retaining density-color field queries and ray compositing. PVD explicitly frames MLP, sparse-tensor, low-rank-tensor, and hash-table implementations as architectures with different trade-offs and reports any-to-any distillation on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples; for example, it reports distilling an MLP NeRF from a hash-table Instant-NGP teacher 10×–20× faster than training the original NeRF from scratch while reaching superior synthesis quality. That result concerns architecture conversion and training speed/quality in PVD's setup, not a change to the foundational emission-absorption equation. assertions.source_quote: The sampling and ray-geometry comparison is especially important for interpreting later results. Original NeRF casts a single ray per pixel and uses hundreds of point samples; hierarchical sampling first evaluates a coarse network and then allocates more fine samples to intervals with visible content. Mip-NeRF changes the query itself by rendering anti-aliased conical frustums rather than infinitesimal point rays. On the dataset presented with NeRF, mip-NeRF reports a 17% reduction in average error rates while being 7% faster and half the size; on a challenging multiscale variant it reports a 60% error reduction, and it matches a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster. These figures are evidence for scale-aware anti-aliasing under mip-NeRF's datasets and implementation, not evidence that the original NeRF integral is incorrect for its matched-scale setting. assertions.source_quote: Computational-cost comparisons should likewise be tied to the exact acceleration mechanism. The original rendering loop evaluates a large MLP at many samples for each pixel, which acceleration literature identifies as too slow for interactive visualization. SNeRG's baking and deferred-rendering approach is reported to increase NeRF rendering speed by three orders of magnitude, but it also introduces a sparse voxel-grid representation with opacity, diffuse color, and learned features plus substantial GPU-memory requirements; NerfAcc reports 1.5×–20× training-time reductions across several NeRF methods by improving sampling through a flexible transmittance-estimator toolbox. These speedups are not directly comparable to each other or to vanilla NeRF quality without matching hardware, resolution, scene sets, memory budgets, sampling counts, and implementation. assertions.source_quote: Geometry-oriented experiments also measure something distinct from photometric novel-view quality. NeRF++ identifies a shape-radiance ambiguity, meaning that view-dependent color and density can jointly explain a finite image set in ways that do not uniquely determine geometry. VDN-NeRF targets this issue under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting, reporting that view-dependence normalization improves geometry without changing the volume-rendering pipeline and can be applied to various baselines, including data captured under a moving light source. Those findings should not be read as a direct PSNR comparison with foundational NeRF: the task includes geometry quality and challenging illumination, and the cited snippets do not supply matched metric values for all methods. assertions.source_quote: Transport-model comparisons are similarly non-equivalent. The foundational renderer accumulates locally predicted emitted color and density along a camera ray; it does not explicitly trace reflection rays or simulate multiple scattering in participating media. Reflection-ray NeRF variants target consistent specular reflections of nearby content while avoiding repeated expensive outgoing-radiance network queries, and physically based differentiable volume renderers coupled with diffusion priors target cloud-like fields where multiple scattering and unknown background radiance matter. In the cloud study, the diffusion prior is trained on 1,000 synthetic volumetric density fields and the renderer supplies gradients for light transport in latent space. Such results cannot establish superiority for ordinary bounded static view synthesis because the optics, priors, datasets, and reconstruction target differ. assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is computational cost, and it follows directly from the foundational rendering loop. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at ordered 3D samples before density and color can be composited. Acceleration literature describes the original process of evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel as too slow for interactive visualization; later systems therefore reduce samples, use transmittance estimators, store features in grids, bake radiance fields, or adopt hash encodings. The implication is not that the continuous-field formulation is invalid, but that photorealistic per-scene optimization and high-resolution rendering carry a substantial sample-evaluation cost unless the storage, sampling, or network architecture is changed. assertions.source_quote: The same posed-image supervision that makes NeRF simple also creates an identifiability problem. Density and view-dependent radiance are optimized jointly from RGB observations, so a finite collection of views can sometimes be explained by different allocations between geometry and appearance. NeRF++ explicitly identifies this as shape-radiance ambiguity, and VDN-NeRF argues that under non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights the ambiguity can affect learned geometry even when rendered images look plausible. The practical implication is that high novel-view fidelity is not equivalent to guaranteed accurate surface reconstruction; geometry-sensitive applications may need normalization, multi-view constraints, depth or mask guidance, or controlled illumination. assertions.source_quote: Point-ray sampling also leaves a multiscale anti-aliasing limitation. NeRF samples a scene with one ray per pixel and queries point locations; mip-NeRF reports that this model can produce excessive blurring or aliasing when training and testing images observe scene content at different resolutions or distances. Supersampling with many rays is expensive because each ray requires hundreds of MLP queries. Mip-NeRF's conical-frustum and integrated-positional-encoding solution changes the query region and scale representation, showing that the original point-sample formulation is not automatically scale-aware even though its underlying alpha-compositing rule remains useful. assertions.source_quote: The foundational emission-absorption renderer is also narrower than a general light-transport simulator. It accumulates locally predicted color and density along a camera ray, with transmittance accounting for earlier occlusion, but it does not inherently trace reflection rays or simulate multiple scattering inside participating media. Reflection-oriented NeRF work targets consistent specular reflections of nearby objects by casting additional rays, while physically based differentiable renderers for cloud-like fields explicitly account for multiple scattering and unknown background radiance. Consequently, the basic equation should not be assumed to model complex interreflection or volumetric scattering accurately merely because it handles view-dependent RGB and partial opacity. assertions.source_quote: Storage and editability create another trade-off in later NeRF architectures, even though they are not defects unique to the original rendering equation. Surveys of acceleration methods distinguish implicit MLP-style fields from explicit or hybrid voxel, sparse-grid, low-rank, and hash-table representations. PVD notes that hash-table-based approaches can train and render faster, but their lack of clear geometric meaning can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing, whereas explicit or hybrid structures can be better suited to geometry-aware manipulation. This means that replacing the MLP solely for speed may improve one axis while worsening interpretability or downstream control; no single cited architecture removes the broader fidelity, memory, and editability trade-off. assertions.source_quote: Sparse and unconstrained observations remain underdetermined without priors. The original method relies on optimizing a separate continuous volume for each scene from a set of calibrated views, whereas pixelNeRF motivates its image-conditioned architecture by noting that independent per-scene optimization requires many calibrated views and substantial compute. When only one or a few views are available, unseen regions cannot be recovered uniquely from the rendering equation alone. Feed-forward features, cross-scene learning, diffusion priors, or other generative assumptions can fill missing information, but they also change the evidence from deterministic multi-view consistency to prior-assisted reconstruction and should not be presented as a capability of minimal NeRF. assertions.source_quote: Finally, the field's success on view synthesis does not imply that its internal representation is universally suitable for every 3D task. Later work notes that NeRF-style implicit fields can deliver excellent rendering while suffering structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation, and dynamic or editing systems add deformation fields, latent codes, mappers, semantic controls, or alternative proxies to obtain controllability. These limitations have concrete consequences: a model optimized to reproduce pixels may not expose editable surfaces, stable correspondences, motion skeletons, or physically meaningful material and lighting factors. The foundational NeRF should therefore be understood as a strong static novel-view-synthesis representation, not as a complete solution to reconstruction, generation, animation, relighting, editing, or real-time graphics by itself. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The first classification criterion is what is being optimized. Foundational NeRF optimizes a continuous, scene-specific neural field implemented by an MLP: a 3D position and 2D viewing direction map to density and view-dependent color. This differs from methods that learn an encoder–decoder to produce a volume from input images, methods that condition a field on one or few images to learn a cross-scene prior, and methods that store substantial scene state in voxels, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, triplanes, or hash tables. These alternatives may still use ray integration, but they do not all share the original plain-MLP, per-scene parameterization. unsupported_claims.source_quote: A second criterion is the geometric query model. The original NeRF casts one infinitesimal ray per pixel and evaluates point samples r(t)=o+td between near and far bounds. Mip-NeRF instead treats the pixel footprint as a conical frustum and uses integrated positional encoding so that scale and aliasing are represented during the field query. That distinction is a change to the queried region and scale model, not merely a faster implementation of the same point-ray query. Likewise, methods that trace reflection rays or model more elaborate light transport extend the transport paths beyond the foundational camera-ray accumulation. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Efficiency should be classified separately from representational semantics. Hash tables, multiresolution feature grids, sparse voxel grids, low-rank tensor factorizations, octrees, baked textures or meshes, and improved transmittance estimators primarily target training cost, rendering speed, memory, or sample allocation. They may preserve NeRF-like alpha compositing while replacing the MLP's parameter storage or reducing the number of field evaluations. unsupported_claims.source_quote: On a computer, the integral is approximated by ray marching through ordered samples. With sample spacing Δt_i, queried density σ_i and queried color c_i, a common piecewise-constant approximation uses sample alpha α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i), transmittance T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and pixel color Ĉ(r)=Σ_i T_iα_i c_i. Equivalently, T_i can be written as Π_{j<i}(1−α_j). The ordering of samples matters because transmittance accumulates opacity from the camera side; the renderer is occlusion-aware while remaining differentiable with respect to the colors and densities predicted by the network. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The first open problem is computational cost, and it follows directly from the foundational rendering loop. Each pixel requires a camera ray, and each ray requires many MLP evaluations at ordered 3D samples before density and color can be composited. Acceleration literature describes the original process of evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel as too slow for interactive visualization; later systems therefore reduce samples, use transmittance estimators, store features in grids, bake radiance fields, or adopt hash encodings. The implication is not that the continuous-field formulation is invalid, but that photorealistic per-scene optimization and high-resolution rendering carry a substantial sample-evaluation cost unless the storage, sampling, or network architecture is changed. unsupported_claims.source_quote: A second limitation is that the basic model is static and scene-specific. The original NeRF is optimized for one scene from posed images and has no native time coordinate, deformation model, image-conditioning network, or cross-scene prior. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The same posed-image supervision that makes NeRF simple also creates an identifiability problem. Density and view-dependent radiance are optimized jointly from RGB observations, so a finite collection of views can sometimes be explained by different allocations between geometry and appearance. NeRF++ explicitly identifies this as shape-radiance ambiguity, and VDN-NeRF argues that under non-Lambertian surfaces and moving lights the ambiguity can affect learned geometry even when rendered images look plausible. The practical implication is that high novel-view fidelity is not equivalent to guaranteed accurate surface reconstruction; geometry-sensitive applications may need normalization, multi-view constraints, depth or mask guidance, or controlled illumination. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Storage and editability create another trade-off in later NeRF architectures, even though they are not defects unique to the original rendering equation. Surveys of acceleration methods distinguish implicit MLP-style fields from explicit or hybrid voxel, sparse-grid, low-rank, and hash-table representations. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Camera assumptions are a further practical boundary. The basic optimization loop requires images with known camera poses so that rays can be cast through the correct pixels and compared with observations. Later work summarized in neural-scene-representation surveys addresses inaccurate or unknown extrinsics and intrinsics by jointly optimizing camera parameters, handles unbounded or large-scale scenes with specialized parameterizations, and accounts for blurred input images by modeling the blur process. These extensions indicate that the clean formulation depends on calibration and capture conditions that real datasets may not satisfy; pose error, scale mismatch, and blur cannot be interpreted as ordinary photometric noise without additional modeling. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Finally, the field's success on view synthesis does not imply that its internal representation is universally suitable for every 3D task. Later work notes that NeRF-style implicit fields can deliver excellent rendering while suffering structural ambiguity that hinders animation and manipulation, and dynamic or editing systems add deformation fields, latent codes, mappers, semantic controls, or alternative proxies to obtain controllability. These limitations have concrete consequences: a model optimized to reproduce pixels may not expose editable surfaces, stable correspondences, motion skeletons, or physically meaningful material and lighting factors. The foundational NeRF should therefore be understood as a strong static novel-view-synthesis representation, not as a complete solution to reconstruction, generation, animation, relighting, editing, or real-time graphics by itself. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The main trade-off is expressivity against cost and scope. Density plus view-dependent color can represent complex, thin, semi-transparent, and non-Lambertian appearance, but per-pixel rays with many MLP evaluations make optimization and rendering sample-heavy. The minimal formulation is also static, per-scene, point-ray based, calibrated-view dependent, and not by itself a solution for acceleration, dynamics, guaranteed surface reconstruction, multiscale anti-aliasing, editing, sparse-view generalization, or full multiple-scattering transport. Later grids, frustum queries, deformation fields, priors, and richer renderers modify storage, sampling, assumptions, or optics rather than redefining the foundational representation itself. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:c893f247624b] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:13:74af091c7378:claim:80f789cfaf48] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:11:c1100a157257:claim:c3e90c0a0be9] [E:arxiv:2112.05139:abstract:claim:acbccae66b53] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:a492f8404c23] [E:arxiv:2310.20710:section:2_2_acceleration_of_nerf_training_and_rendering:0:c9c2ec744ba1:claim:71955da6cf95] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:abstract:claim:9b45ed1368a9] [E:arxiv:2103.13415:section:abstract:1:a3779284c3ef:claim:3a680cb2750e] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:66fffdf9705e] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:5c2f48945a3e] [E:arxiv:2010.07492:section:abstract:0:cf232692f549:claim:2c7c41367a9d] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:1bdffa6903bf] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:386e8a07e8e9] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:abstract:claim:41f46e8862f5] [E:arxiv:2405.14871:abstract:claim:4f475123f295] [E:arxiv:2501.05226:section:abstract:2:b3c9ccfb4665:claim:90f10dbe107d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:dfc8baf4037c] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:97daf41b7e02] [E:arxiv:2012.02190:abstract:claim:e532ea43ef3b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:16:da1471ffddfa:claim:7916a3c45f1e] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:3:604987249f19:claim:556900cfb163] [E:arxiv:2507.11971:abstract:claim:734892b7b3a8] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:6ca968e64c50]
